## Statement

Assume AC. Fix $K\ge1$ and $A>0$. There is a finite $C_{A,K}$ such that the following holds uniformly over $1\le d\le2$, integers $1\le m\le N$, and $B\ge1$. Let $X_1,\ldots,X_m$ be independent centered vectors with representations
$$X_i=Z_i+\sum_{r=1}^{r_i}Y_{ir},\qquad |Y_{ir}|\le B\ \hbox{almost surely},$$
where every $r_i$ is finite, all displayed atom and Gaussian terms are independent, every $Y_{ir}$ is centered, and every $Z_i$ is a centered Gaussian vector, possibly degenerate. Suppose
$$I_d\le D_i:=\operatorname{cov}(X_i)\le KI_d.$$
There is a coupling with independent $G_i\sim N_d(0,D_i)$ satisfying
$$\Pr\!\left(\max_{1\le k\le m}\left|\sum_{i=1}^k(X_i-G_i)\right|>C_{A,K}B\log^3(eN)\right)\le N^{-A}.$$
The constants do not depend on the atom counts or individual laws. Empty atom sums and zero Gaussian terms are allowed.

The coupling laws can be chosen as a measurable probability kernel in a supplied standard Borel parameter $\theta$: if the atom laws and Gaussian covariance matrices are measurable kernels and functions of $\theta$, with the hypotheses holding for each $\theta$, there is a coupling kernel $Q_\theta(dx,dg)$ with the stated product marginals and the displayed bound for each $\theta$. Thus a random environment with these conditional independent atom laws can first be sampled, and this coupling kernel then applied conditionally. This assertion concerns the conditional laws supplied in the hypotheses and does not assume a selection of regular conditional laws separately at each parameter.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The atom and Gaussian representations, covariance bounds, parameters $A,K,d,m,N,B$, and, for the kernel assertion, the supplied measurable atom laws and Gaussian covariance matrices. Matrix inequalities are quadratic form inequalities and all vector norms are Euclidean.

[A1] AC is assumed. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] Independent sums of centered bounded vectors and a Gaussian, of total covariance $sI_j$ and Gaussian covariance at least $\gamma sI_j$, have the uniform cumulant and tilted Fourier bounds of [[lem-gaussian-anchored-sums-have-cumulant-and-fourier-bounds]].

[F2] The Gaussian anchored conditional quantile supplier constructs measurable root transports and, for joint dimension $2d\le4$, measurable transports of a fresh independent Gaussian residual conditional on the target parent. With covariance $sI$, atom bound $b$, and Gaussian covariance fraction $\gamma>0$, the target value error is bounded by $C_\gamma b(1+(|p|^2+|v|^2)/s)$ when $s\ge C_\gamma b^2$ and $|p|,|v|\le c_\gamma s/b$. [[lem-gaussian-anchored-conditional-quantile-coupling]]

[F3] Real symmetric matrices have an orthonormal eigenbasis. [[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]]

[F4] A Gaussian has its covariance characteristic function; zero cross covariance implies independence for Gaussian subvectors by factorization. A positive definite Gaussian has its Gaussian density. [[lem-characteristic-function-of-a-multivariate-normal-law]], [[thm-nondegenerate-multivariate-normal-law-has-density]]

[F5] Integrating a measurable function against a supplied probability kernel is measurable, and finite products of probability kernels are probability kernels. [[thm-measurability-of-integration-against-a-kernel]], [[lem-finite-products-of-probability-kernels]]

[F6] Nonnegative integrals obey Tonelli and monotone convergence. [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]], [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]

[F7] A kernel extension depending only on one part of an independent pair preserves independence from its complement. [[lem-conditional-independence-under-kernel-extension-and-conditioning]]

[F8] Exponential Markov bounds, the finite union bound, and Euclidean triangle inequality apply. [[cor-markov-inequality-for-random-variables]], [[thm-finite-union-bound]], [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]

[F9] Expectations of finite products of nonnegative functions of independent variables factor. [[thm-factorization-of-expectations-for-independent-variables]]

## Proof

1.1 For a coordinate $Y$ of one centered atom, $E|Y|^r\le B^{r-2}EY^2$ for every integer $r\ge2$. Absolute exponential-series integration is legitimate because $\sum_r|hY|^r/r!\le e^{B|h|}$; [F6] permits summing its nonnegative absolute terms, and its positive and negative parts then give the signed series identity. For $B|h|<1$, centering cancels the linear term and $r!\ge2$ for $r\ge2$, so
$$\log Ee^{hY}\le Ee^{hY}-1\le\frac{h^2EY^2}{2(1-B|h|)}.$$
A centered Gaussian coordinate has logarithmic mgf $h^2\operatorname{var}(Z)/2$, by completing the square in its positive-variance eigencoordinates using [F3] and [F4]; zero-variance coordinates vanish. Independence multiplies the finitely many atom and Gaussian mgfs. Since their variances add to each coordinate variance of $X_i$, at most $K$, any sum of $s$ entries, also with arbitrary matching Gaussian replacements, has coordinate log mgf at most $Ks h^2/[2(1-B|h|)]$. For a coordinate threshold $u>0$ use $h=u/(Ks+Bu)$ and exponential Markov for both signs. This gives tail at most $2\exp\{-u^2/[2(Ks+Bu)]\}$. The coordinate union bound therefore gives, uniformly in atom counts,
$$\Pr\!\left(\left|\sum_{i\in I}X_i\right|>C_K[\sqrt{st}+Bt]\right)\le C_K e^{-c_Kt},\qquad t\ge1.$$
This holds for every contiguous interval in any compressed ordering. [given, A1, F3, F4, F6, F8, F9, algebra]

1.2 Consider a dyadic mixed row whose odd entries are independent matching Gaussians and whose even entries have their raw laws. At a node of $s\ge4$ entries let its two child covariance matrices be $U,V$, put $W=U+V$, and, for its target child sums $S_L,S_R$, define
$$P=S_L+S_R,\qquad H=UW^{-1},\qquad D=S_L-HP,\qquad R=U-UW^{-1}U.$$
Independence gives $\operatorname{cov}(P)=W$, $\operatorname{cov}(P,D)=U-WW^{-1}U=0$, and $\operatorname{cov}(D)=R$. The symmetric matrix $R$ equals $UW^{-1}V$ and has inverse $V^{-1}WU^{-1}=U^{-1}+V^{-1}$; hence it is positive definite without assuming commutation. Since each child has $s/2$ entries, [F3] gives
$$\tfrac s2I\le U,V\le\tfrac{Ks}2I,\qquad sI\le W\le KsI,\qquad \tfrac s4I\le R\le\tfrac{Ks}4I.$$
The final inequalities follow by inverting, adding, and reinverting the quadratic form bounds. [given, F3, algebra]

1.3 The transformed pair $Q=\sqrt s\operatorname{diag}(W^{-1/2},R^{-1/2})(P,D)$ has covariance $sI_{2d}$. A raw atom $x$ in its left or right child contributes respectively
$$\sqrt s\bigl(W^{-1/2}x,R^{-1/2}VW^{-1}x\bigr),\qquad \sqrt s\bigl(W^{-1/2}x,-R^{-1/2}UW^{-1}x\bigr).$$
Their norms are at most $C_KB$, since $\sqrt s\|W^{-1/2}\|\le1$, $\sqrt s\|R^{-1/2}\|\le2$, and $\|UW^{-1}\|,\|VW^{-1}\|\le K/2$. Each child contains half Gaussian entries, so its Gaussian covariance is at least $(s/4)I$, at least $\gamma$ times its total covariance with $\gamma=1/(2K)$. Congruence of quadratic forms therefore makes the Gaussian covariance of $Q$ at least $\gamma sI_{2d}$. All its bounded contributions are the independently transformed original atoms, and all Gaussian contributions combine into an independent Gaussian. Thus [F1] and [F2] apply directly to $Q$, including its coordinate prefixes. The conditioning is on its first $d$ coordinates. Undoing the separate parent and residual whitening, whose inverse norms are bounded by $C_K$, gives a transport of a fresh $E_I\sim N_d(0,R)$ to $D$ conditional on $P=p$, with error
$$|T_{I,p}(E_I)-E_I|\le C_KB\left(1+\frac{|p|^2+|T_{I,p}(E_I)|^2}{s}\right)$$
when $s\ge C_KB^2$ and the two target norms are at most $c_Ks/B$. The root has the analogous transport from $N_d(0,W)$ with error $C_KB(1+|P|^2/s)$. There is no additional factor from the atom counts or from $\sqrt s$. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.2, algebra]

2.1 Temporarily take a dyadic current length $q\le2N$, set $L=a\log(eN)$, and let $q_0$ be the least dyadic integer at least $H_KB^2L$, with $H_K$ to be fixed. Suppose $q\ge2q_0$. Start with an independent Gaussian row having the individual covariances $D_i$. Its root sum and residuals $E_I=V_L-UW^{-1}V_I$ at the active nodes are mutually independent Gaussian vectors of covariances $W_{\rm root}$ and $R_I$: the cross covariances vanish, and independence follows recursively from [F4]. Apply the root transport in step 1.3 and then, descending the tree, set $D_I=T_{I,S_I}(E_I)$ and
$$S_L=UW^{-1}S_I+D_I,\quad S_R=VW^{-1}S_I-D_I,\quad V_L=UW^{-1}V_I+E_I,\quad V_R=VW^{-1}V_I-E_I.$$
Stop at length $q_0$. Each fresh residual is independent of the already exposed parents, so every target split has exactly its prescribed conditional law. For Gaussians the child covariance is $UW^{-1}U+R=U$ and the cross covariance is $UW^{-1}V-R=0$, with the analogous right covariance $V$. [F2, F4, step 1.2, step 1.3, construct, choose, algebra]

2.2 There is an explicit terminal target kernel, also measurable in any supplied environment. In a terminal mixed block let $\mu$ be the product law of its raw positions, let $s(r)$ be their sum, and let $G>0$ be the sum of the matching Gaussian-position covariances. Given the target block sum $u$, sample the raw-position vector from
$$\frac{q_G(u-s(r))\,\mu(dr)}{\int q_G(u-s(v))\,\mu(dv)}.$$
The denominator is finite and strictly positive everywhere by [F4]. Fill the Gaussian positions conditional on their remaining sum $u-s(r)$: for their covariance matrices $C_j$ and fresh independent $h_j\sim N(0,C_j)$, put $H_0=\sum_jh_j$ and $g_j=C_jG^{-1}(u-s(r))+h_j-C_jG^{-1}H_0$. The residual vector has sum zero, zero cross covariance with $H_0$, and covariance blocks $\delta_{ij}C_i-C_iG^{-1}C_j$; thus [F4] identifies its Gaussian conditional law. Multiplying the posterior by the total-sum density and integrating in $u$ proves the original raw/Gaussian product law, first on rectangles and then by monotone approximation. This verifies the terminal conditional law at every sum, without choosing regular conditional versions. Independent terminal kernels and the split laws of step 2.1 consequently recover exactly the entire mixed row product law by induction through the disjoint binary blocks. The existing Gaussian row is unchanged, and already has its required product law. [F4, F5, F6, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 Use step 1.1 and a union bound for every dyadic target sum and every within-terminal prefix in the completed target and Gaussian rows. There are at most $Cq$ such vectors. Except on probability $C_Kq e^{-c_KL}$, each target sum of size $s$ has norm at most $C_K(\sqrt{sL}+BL)$. The target residual is $D_I=VW^{-1}S_L-UW^{-1}S_R$, so its norm satisfies the same bound with a different $C_K$. At active sizes $s\ge2q_0$, choose $H_K$ large enough that these target norms are at most $c_Ks/B$; their ratios to $s/B$ are bounded by $C_K/\sqrt{H_K}+C_K/H_K$. Their squared norms divided by $s$ are at most $C_KL$. Step 1.3 therefore bounds the root discrepancy and every residual discrepancy $\delta_I=D_I-E_I$ by $C_KBL$. The within-terminal prefix norms are at most $C_K(\sqrt{q_0L}+BL)\le C_KBL$, since $q_0<2H_KB^2L$. No conditional concentration inside a terminal block has been assumed. [F8, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 2.2, choose, algebra]

3.2 Write $e_I=S_I-V_I$. Its child equations are $e_L=UW^{-1}e_I+\delta_I$ and $e_R=VW^{-1}e_I-\delta_I$. For a prefix $P$ ending at a terminal boundary of $I$, let $C_P$ be the sum of its individual covariance matrices. Its discrepancy has the exact expansion
$$\sum_{i\in P}(X_i-G_i)=C_PW_I^{-1}e_I+\sum_{J\text{ on the boundary path}}M_{J,P}\delta_J.$$
If the boundary lies in the left child, $M_{J,P}=C_{\rm partial\ left}W_{J_L}^{-1}$; if it lies in the right child, $M_{J,P}=I-C_{\rm partial\ right}W_{J_R}^{-1}$. To prove the formula, in the left case substitute the child's leading term $C_PU^{-1}e_L$ and cancel $U^{-1}U$; in the right case add $e_L$ to $C_QV^{-1}e_R$, obtaining leading coefficient $(U+C_Q)W^{-1}$ and residual coefficient $I-C_QV^{-1}$. Induction from terminal blocks proves the expansion. This cancellation uses the order $W_{\rm desc}W_{\rm parent}^{-1}W_{\rm parent}W_{\rm grandparent}^{-1}$ and never commutes two matrices. If a partial child has $r$ of its $h$ entries, its coefficient norm is at most $Kr/h\le K$. Hence $\|M_{J,P}\|\le1+K$ and $\|C_PW_I^{-1}\|\le K$. There are at most $\log_2q$ boundary ancestors. The expansion and step 3.1 give terminal-boundary error $C_KBL\log(eq)$; adding its terminal prefix residual gives the same bound for all prefixes. [F8, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

3.3 If $q<2q_0$, couple a raw or mixed row independently to a matching Gaussian row. Their unconditional concentration bounds from step 1.1 and a union bound over prefixes give maximum discrepancy at most $C_K(\sqrt{qL}+BL)\le C_KBL$ except on probability $C_Kq e^{-c_KL}$. This covers the small sizes, including a row of one entry, and large $B$. Thus in all cases a mixed row can be coupled directly to an already realized matching Gaussian row with stage error at most $C_KBL\log(eq)$ and bad probability at most $C_Kq e^{-c_KL}$. [F8, step 1.1, step 3.2, algebra]

4.1 Pad the initial length $m$ to dyadic $q<2m$ by independent $N_d(0,I_d)$ entries; for $m=1$ take $q=1$. These added laws have empty atom sums and preserve all covariance bounds. Begin with its matching independent Gaussian row. At an active length at least $2q_0$, apply steps 2.1–3.2, taking the target laws to be the designated raw laws in even slots and matching Gaussians in odd slots. Use the root and residual primitives computed from the already realized active Gaussian row, and fresh target terminal kernels. Freeze the newly raw even positions and retain the odd Gaussian positions in their compressed order. Their covariance matrices still lie between $I$ and $KI$. The target product law and [F7] preserve independence of the active row from its frozen complement. At an active length below $2q_0$, independently replace all remaining Gaussian positions by their designated raw laws, using step 3.3, and stop. This constructs the full intended independent raw row after at most $C\log(eN)$ stages, without changing the original Gaussian row. [F5, F7, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 3.3, construct]

4.2 Every original prefix meets the active positions of each stage in an initial compressed prefix. Triangle inequality adds the stage maximum errors, each at most $C_KBL\log(eN)$, to give total error at most $C_{A,K}B\log^3(eN)$. Always use the ambient $L=a\log(eN)$, even for short compressed rows. The union bad probability is at most $C_KN\log(eN)e^{-c_Ka\log(eN)}$. Choose $a$ sufficiently large depending only on $A,K$ to make this at most $N^{-A}$ for all $N\ge1$; then restrict to the first $m$ entries. This proves the numerical assertion. [F8, step 3.3, step 4.1, choose, algebra]

5.1 For the parameter assertion, every entry law is a measurable kernel obtained by applying addition to the finite product of its supplied atom and Gaussian kernels, using [F5]. Covariance entries are measurable integrals. In dimensions one and two positive definite inverse square roots are continuous functions of their matrices: in dimension two, for $C>0$, $C^{1/2}=(C+\sqrt{\det C}\,I)/\sqrt{\operatorname{tr}C+2\sqrt{\det C}}$, as verified in an eigenbasis by [F3]; the semidefinite zero case is defined by zero and the formula extends continuously. Thus the Gaussian starts and all transforms in steps 1.2–1.3 depend measurably on the parameter. Mixed transformed joint and prefix densities are Gaussian convolution integrals of their raw product kernels, so are jointly measurable by [F5] and strictly positive. Their conditional CDFs are measurable density-ratio integrals. The coordinate quantiles in [F2] are measurable rational infima of those CDFs; hence its root and residual maps are jointly measurable in the parameter and all spatial inputs. The terminal posterior in step 2.2 is likewise a measurable kernel with positive measurable denominator, followed by the explicit Gaussian bridge kernel. Finite kernel products and successive extensions preserve measurability: for one extension define its law by integrating the next kernel against the preceding law; [F5] gives measurable evaluations and [F6] gives countable additivity by monotone convergence of disjoint indicator sums. Iterating this finite construction gives a coupling kernel $Q_\theta$, and every previous marginal and probability bound holds at each parameter. No pointwise selection of conditional-law versions or coupling laws is used. [A1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 2.2, step 4.2, construct, algebra] ∎

## Source notes

The source supplies the dyadic conditional-quantile architecture. The heterogeneous covariance formula in step 3.2, the stopped Gaussian-anchor replacement, and the parameterwise terminal posterior are proved locally. The bound is deliberately weaker than the source's optimized strong approximation estimates. Whole grouped entries need not be bounded: the boundedness hypothesis concerns their independent centered atoms.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Fix $0<\gamma\le1$. Let $1\le d\le4$, $s>0$, $B>0$, and let $X_1,\ldots,X_m,Z$ be independent centered random vectors in $\mathbb R^d$, where $m\ge0$, $|X_j|\le B$ almost surely, and $Z\sim N_d(0,G)$. Suppose $S=Z+\sum_jX_j$ has covariance $sI_d$ and $G\ge\gamma sI_d$ in quadratic form order. There is an absolute constant $C_0\ge1$ such that, with $\tau=C_0B$, the logarithmic moment generating function
$$K(z)=\log\mathbb E e^{z\cdot S},\qquad K(0)=0,$$
has a single analytic branch on the complex Euclidean ball $\tau|z|<1$, and
$$|\partial_u\partial_v^2K(z)|\le\tau s|u||v|^2\qquad(u,v\in\mathbb R^d,\ \tau|z|<1).$$
Here $z\cdot S$ uses the complex bilinear dot product and $|z|^2=\sum_i|z_i|^2$. Every real exponential tilt $\mathbb P_h(d\omega)=e^{h\cdot S-K(h)}\mathbb P(d\omega)$ is defined, and its characteristic function satisfies
$$|\varphi_h(t)|:=|\mathbb E_h e^{it\cdot S}|\le e^{-\gamma s|t|^2/2}\qquad(t,h\in\mathbb R^d),$$
where $K(h)=\log\mathbb E e^{h\cdot S}$ for real $h$, also outside the analytic ball. Put $\kappa=\tau/\sqrt s$. For every fixed $a>0$ and integer $N\ge1$ there is a finite $C_{a,N,\gamma}$, uniform in $1\le d\le4$, such that, if $0<\kappa\le1$,
$$(2\pi)^{-d}\int_{|t|\ge a/\tau}|\varphi_h(t)|\,dt\le C_{a,N,\gamma}\kappa^Ns^{-d/2},$$
$$(2\pi)^{-d}\int_{|t|\ge a/\tau}|t\cdot v||\varphi_h(t)|\,dt\le C_{a,N,\gamma}\kappa^N|v|s^{-(d+1)/2}.$$
All assertions hold with the same $C_0$, $B$, $s$, and $\gamma$ for $AS$, where $A$ is any real $k\times d$ matrix with $1\le k\le d$ and $AA^T=I_k$. This includes every coordinate prefix, every orthogonal change of coordinates, and their compositions. In particular it covers the normalized joint sum and difference of two independent children by applying the assertion in their joint dimension, provided that dimension is at most four and the joint input satisfies the stated covariance assumptions.

Assume AC and the hypotheses of [[lem-gaussian-anchored-sums-have-cumulant-and-fourier-bounds]]: $S=Z+\sum_{i=1}^mX_i\in\mathbb R^d$, $1\le d\le4$, the centered summands are independent, $|X_i|\le B$, $Z$ is Gaussian with covariance $G\ge\gamma sI_d$, and $\operatorname{cov}(S)=sI_d$, where $s,B>0$ and $0<\gamma\le1$. Put $\tau=C_0B$, with $C_0$ from that supplier, and let $\Phi_s$ be the CDF of $N(0,s)$. There are constants $c_\gamma>0$ and $C_\gamma<\infty$, independent of the summand laws, $m,d,s,B$, with the following properties.

For $1\le j\le d$, let $H_j(x',y)$ be the conditional CDF of $S_j$ given $S_{<j}=x'\in\mathbb R^{j-1}$ obtained by dividing the joint prefix density by its marginal density. These densities are strictly positive, so this defines a probability kernel at every $x'$, including prefixes of probability zero. Its quantile transport
$$T_j(x',z)=H_j(x',\cdot)^{-1}(\Phi_s(z))$$
is jointly Borel measurable and takes a fresh $N(0,s)$ variable to that conditional law. If $s\ge C_\gamma\tau^2$, then, with $y=T_j(x',z)$,
$$|y-z|\le C_\gamma\tau\left(1+\frac{|x'|^2+y^2}{s}\right)\quad\hbox{when }|x'|+|y|\le c_\gamma s/\tau,$$
and also
$$|T_j(x',z)-z|\le C_\gamma\tau\left(1+\frac{|x'|^2+z^2}{s}\right)\quad\hbox{when }|x'|+|z|\le c_\gamma s/\tau.$$
For $j=1$, the prefix is empty and its norm is zero. The resulting successive coordinate transport $R$ sends $N_d(0,sI_d)$ to the law of $S$ and satisfies
$$|R(g)-g|\le C_\gamma\tau\left(1+\frac{|R(g)|^2}{s}\right)\quad\hbox{when }|R(g)|\le c_\gamma s/\tau.$$

If $d=2a$ with $a\le2$, write $S=(P,D)$ with $P,D\in\mathbb R^a$. The last $a$ successive conditional transports give a jointly measurable $T_p$ taking a fresh $E\sim N_a(0,sI_a)$ to the conditional law of $D$ given $P=p$, and
$$|T_p(e)-e|\le C_\gamma\tau\left(1+\frac{|p|^2+|T_p(e)|^2}{s}\right)$$
when $s\ge C_\gamma\tau^2$ and $|p|,|T_p(e)|\le c_\gamma s/\tau$. The Gaussian reference bridge $E$ is independent of its Gaussian parent.

There is also the following scalar unequal-variance form. Let $L,R$ be independent centered scalar sums of independent variables bounded by $B$ and independent Gaussian terms, with variances $V_L,V_R\in[s/2,s]$, and with Gaussian component variances at least $\gamma V_L,\gamma V_R$, respectively. Put
$$W=V_L+V_R,\qquad w=V_L/W,\qquad v=V_LV_R/W,\qquad P=L+R,\qquad D=L-wP.$$
Then $W\in[s,2s]$, $w\in[1/3,2/3]$, $v\in[s/4,s/2]$. There is a jointly measurable transport taking a fresh $N(0,v)$ variable to $D$ conditional on $P=p$ with
$$|T_p(e)-e|\le C_\gamma\tau\left(1+\frac{p^2+T_p(e)^2}{s}\right)$$
when $s\ge C_\gamma\tau^2$ and $|p|,|T_p(e)|\le c_\gamma s/\tau$. The corresponding root transport from $N(0,W)$ to $P$ obeys the analogous bound with $|P|^2/s$. The reconstructed children are $L=wP+D$ and $R=(1-w)P-D$.

All these maps are jointly measurable in an additional measurable parameter whenever, on each fixed finite row length, the bounded input laws are probability kernels, their Gaussian covariance and $s$ are measurable functions, and the displayed hypotheses hold parameterwise. This includes countable arrays with different row lengths. No claim here asserts the conditional estimates for raw bounded laws without a positive Gaussian component.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

Assume AC. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then $$\Phi_X(t):=\mathbb E e^{it\cdot X}=\exp(it\cdot m-t^T\Sigma t/2)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R^d).$$ This transform uniquely determines the law, including singular Sigma.

Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$, $m\in\mathbb R^d$, and let $\Sigma$ be a real symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then its law has Lebesgue density
$$f_{m,\Sigma}(x)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}\det(\Sigma)^{-1/2} \exp\!\left(-\tfrac12(x-m)^T\Sigma^{-1}(x-m)\right), \qquad x\in\mathbb R^d.$$

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

Let $(S,\Sigma)$ and $(T_i,\Tau_i)$ for $i<n$ be measurable spaces, with
$n<\infty$, and let $K_i:S\to T_i$ be probability kernels with the same
source. There is a unique probability kernel
$$K:S\to\prod_{i<n}T_i$$
whose evaluation on every measurable rectangle is
$$K(s,\prod_{i<n}B_i)=\prod_{i<n}K_i(s,B_i).$$
For $n=0$, the target is the empty-product singleton and $K$ is its point
mass. For $n>0$, the product sigma-algebra is the recursive finite product
sigma-algebra.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Assume AC. Let $L,R,C,V$ be random elements in arbitrary measurable spaces. Suppose $L\perp\!\!\!\perp R\mid\sigma(C)$ and that the joint law of $(L,R,C,V)$ is obtained from the law of $(L,R,C)$ by a probability kernel $K(l,c,dv)$ depending only on $(l,c)$. Then
$$(L,V)\perp\!\!\!\perp R\mid\sigma(C),\qquad L\perp\!\!\!\perp R\mid\sigma(C,V).$$
No regular conditional law on an unspecified measurable space is assumed: $K$ is supplied in the hypotheses.

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

For every finite family of events $A_0,\ldots,A_{n-1}$,
$$\mathbb P\!\left(\bigcup_{i<n}A_i\right)\le\sum_{i<n}\mathbb P(A_i).$$
For $n=0$ both sides are $0$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Let $n\ge1$, let $X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}$ be independent real random variables on a
common probability space, and let $g_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be Borel
measurable for each $i<n$.

1. If every $g_i$ is nonnegative, then
   $$\mathbb E\left[\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)\right]=\prod_{i<n}\mathbb E[g_i(X_i)]$$
   in $[0,+\infty]$. In this finite product of expectations, a zero factor
   makes the product zero even when another factor is $+\infty$; otherwise
   multiplication has its usual extended nonnegative meaning.
2. If every $g_i(X_i)$ is integrable, then $\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)$ is integrable
   and the same factorization holds in $\mathbb R$.

derivations.claim:
For a coordinate $Y$ of one centered atom, $E|Y|^r\le B^{r-2}EY^2$ for every integer $r\ge2$. Absolute exponential-series integration is legitimate because $\sum_r|hY|^r/r!\le e^{B|h|}$; [F6] permits summing its nonnegative absolute terms, and its positive and negative parts then give the signed series identity. For $B|h|<1$, centering cancels the linear term and $r!\ge2$ for $r\ge2$, so
$$\log Ee^{hY}\le Ee^{hY}-1\le\frac{h^2EY^2}{2(1-B|h|)}.$$
A centered Gaussian coordinate has logarithmic mgf $h^2\operatorname{var}(Z)/2$, by completing the square in its positive-variance eigencoordinates using [F3] and [F4]; zero-variance coordinates vanish. Independence multiplies the finitely many atom and Gaussian mgfs. Since their variances add to each coordinate variance of $X_i$, at most $K$, any sum of $s$ entries, also with arbitrary matching Gaussian replacements, has coordinate log mgf at most $Ks h^2/[2(1-B|h|)]$. For a coordinate threshold $u>0$ use $h=u/(Ks+Bu)$ and exponential Markov for both signs. This gives tail at most $2\exp\{-u^2/[2(Ks+Bu)]\}$. The coordinate union bound therefore gives, uniformly in atom counts,
$$\Pr\!\left(\left|\sum_{i\in I}X_i\right|>C_K[\sqrt{st}+Bt]\right)\le C_K e^{-c_Kt},\qquad t\ge1.$$
This holds for every contiguous interval in any compressed ordering.

Consider a dyadic mixed row whose odd entries are independent matching Gaussians and whose even entries have their raw laws. At a node of $s\ge4$ entries let its two child covariance matrices be $U,V$, put $W=U+V$, and, for its target child sums $S_L,S_R$, define
$$P=S_L+S_R,\qquad H=UW^{-1},\qquad D=S_L-HP,\qquad R=U-UW^{-1}U.$$
Independence gives $\operatorname{cov}(P)=W$, $\operatorname{cov}(P,D)=U-WW^{-1}U=0$, and $\operatorname{cov}(D)=R$. The symmetric matrix $R$ equals $UW^{-1}V$ and has inverse $V^{-1}WU^{-1}=U^{-1}+V^{-1}$; hence it is positive definite without assuming commutation. Since each child has $s/2$ entries, [F3] gives
$$\tfrac s2I\le U,V\le\tfrac{Ks}2I,\qquad sI\le W\le KsI,\qquad \tfrac s4I\le R\le\tfrac{Ks}4I.$$
The final inequalities follow by inverting, adding, and reinverting the quadratic form bounds.

The transformed pair $Q=\sqrt s\operatorname{diag}(W^{-1/2},R^{-1/2})(P,D)$ has covariance $sI_{2d}$. A raw atom $x$ in its left or right child contributes respectively
$$\sqrt s\bigl(W^{-1/2}x,R^{-1/2}VW^{-1}x\bigr),\qquad \sqrt s\bigl(W^{-1/2}x,-R^{-1/2}UW^{-1}x\bigr).$$
Their norms are at most $C_KB$, since $\sqrt s\|W^{-1/2}\|\le1$, $\sqrt s\|R^{-1/2}\|\le2$, and $\|UW^{-1}\|,\|VW^{-1}\|\le K/2$. Each child contains half Gaussian entries, so its Gaussian covariance is at least $(s/4)I$, at least $\gamma$ times its total covariance with $\gamma=1/(2K)$. Congruence of quadratic forms therefore makes the Gaussian covariance of $Q$ at least $\gamma sI_{2d}$. All its bounded contributions are the independently transformed original atoms, and all Gaussian contributions combine into an independent Gaussian. Thus [F1] and [F2] apply directly to $Q$, including its coordinate prefixes. The conditioning is on its first $d$ coordinates. Undoing the separate parent and residual whitening, whose inverse norms are bounded by $C_K$, gives a transport of a fresh $E_I\sim N_d(0,R)$ to $D$ conditional on $P=p$, with error
$$|T_{I,p}(E_I)-E_I|\le C_KB\left(1+\frac{|p|^2+|T_{I,p}(E_I)|^2}{s}\right)$$
when $s\ge C_KB^2$ and the two target norms are at most $c_Ks/B$. The root has the analogous transport from $N_d(0,W)$ with error $C_KB(1+|P|^2/s)$. There is no additional factor from the atom counts or from $\sqrt s$.

Temporarily take a dyadic current length $q\le2N$, set $L=a\log(eN)$, and let $q_0$ be the least dyadic integer at least $H_KB^2L$, with $H_K$ to be fixed. Suppose $q\ge2q_0$. Start with an independent Gaussian row having the individual covariances $D_i$. Its root sum and residuals $E_I=V_L-UW^{-1}V_I$ at the active nodes are mutually independent Gaussian vectors of covariances $W_{\rm root}$ and $R_I$: the cross covariances vanish, and independence follows recursively from [F4]. Apply the root transport in step 1.3 and then, descending the tree, set $D_I=T_{I,S_I}(E_I)$ and
$$S_L=UW^{-1}S_I+D_I,\quad S_R=VW^{-1}S_I-D_I,\quad V_L=UW^{-1}V_I+E_I,\quad V_R=VW^{-1}V_I-E_I.$$
Stop at length $q_0$. Each fresh residual is independent of the already exposed parents, so every target split has exactly its prescribed conditional law. For Gaussians the child covariance is $UW^{-1}U+R=U$ and the cross covariance is $UW^{-1}V-R=0$, with the analogous right covariance $V$.

There is an explicit terminal target kernel, also measurable in any supplied environment. In a terminal mixed block let $\mu$ be the product law of its raw positions, let $s(r)$ be their sum, and let $G>0$ be the sum of the matching Gaussian-position covariances. Given the target block sum $u$, sample the raw-position vector from
$$\frac{q_G(u-s(r))\,\mu(dr)}{\int q_G(u-s(v))\,\mu(dv)}.$$
The denominator is finite and strictly positive everywhere by [F4]. Fill the Gaussian positions conditional on their remaining sum $u-s(r)$: for their covariance matrices $C_j$ and fresh independent $h_j\sim N(0,C_j)$, put $H_0=\sum_jh_j$ and $g_j=C_jG^{-1}(u-s(r))+h_j-C_jG^{-1}H_0$. The residual vector has sum zero, zero cross covariance with $H_0$, and covariance blocks $\delta_{ij}C_i-C_iG^{-1}C_j$; thus [F4] identifies its Gaussian conditional law. Multiplying the posterior by the total-sum density and integrating in $u$ proves the original raw/Gaussian product law, first on rectangles and then by monotone approximation. This verifies the terminal conditional law at every sum, without choosing regular conditional versions. Independent terminal kernels and the split laws of step 2.1 consequently recover exactly the entire mixed row product law by induction through the disjoint binary blocks. The existing Gaussian row is unchanged, and already has its required product law.

Use step 1.1 and a union bound for every dyadic target sum and every within-terminal prefix in the completed target and Gaussian rows. There are at most $Cq$ such vectors. Except on probability $C_Kq e^{-c_KL}$, each target sum of size $s$ has norm at most $C_K(\sqrt{sL}+BL)$. The target residual is $D_I=VW^{-1}S_L-UW^{-1}S_R$, so its norm satisfies the same bound with a different $C_K$. At active sizes $s\ge2q_0$, choose $H_K$ large enough that these target norms are at most $c_Ks/B$; their ratios to $s/B$ are bounded by $C_K/\sqrt{H_K}+C_K/H_K$. Their squared norms divided by $s$ are at most $C_KL$. Step 1.3 therefore bounds the root discrepancy and every residual discrepancy $\delta_I=D_I-E_I$ by $C_KBL$. The within-terminal prefix norms are at most $C_K(\sqrt{q_0L}+BL)\le C_KBL$, since $q_0<2H_KB^2L$. No conditional concentration inside a terminal block has been assumed.

Write $e_I=S_I-V_I$. Its child equations are $e_L=UW^{-1}e_I+\delta_I$ and $e_R=VW^{-1}e_I-\delta_I$. For a prefix $P$ ending at a terminal boundary of $I$, let $C_P$ be the sum of its individual covariance matrices. Its discrepancy has the exact expansion
$$\sum_{i\in P}(X_i-G_i)=C_PW_I^{-1}e_I+\sum_{J\text{ on the boundary path}}M_{J,P}\delta_J.$$
If the boundary lies in the left child, $M_{J,P}=C_{\rm partial\ left}W_{J_L}^{-1}$; if it lies in the right child, $M_{J,P}=I-C_{\rm partial\ right}W_{J_R}^{-1}$. To prove the formula, in the left case substitute the child's leading term $C_PU^{-1}e_L$ and cancel $U^{-1}U$; in the right case add $e_L$ to $C_QV^{-1}e_R$, obtaining leading coefficient $(U+C_Q)W^{-1}$ and residual coefficient $I-C_QV^{-1}$. Induction from terminal blocks proves the expansion. This cancellation uses the order $W_{\rm desc}W_{\rm parent}^{-1}W_{\rm parent}W_{\rm grandparent}^{-1}$ and never commutes two matrices. If a partial child has $r$ of its $h$ entries, its coefficient norm is at most $Kr/h\le K$. Hence $\|M_{J,P}\|\le1+K$ and $\|C_PW_I^{-1}\|\le K$. There are at most $\log_2q$ boundary ancestors. The expansion and step 3.1 give terminal-boundary error $C_KBL\log(eq)$; adding its terminal prefix residual gives the same bound for all prefixes.

If $q<2q_0$, couple a raw or mixed row independently to a matching Gaussian row. Their unconditional concentration bounds from step 1.1 and a union bound over prefixes give maximum discrepancy at most $C_K(\sqrt{qL}+BL)\le C_KBL$ except on probability $C_Kq e^{-c_KL}$. This covers the small sizes, including a row of one entry, and large $B$. Thus in all cases a mixed row can be coupled directly to an already realized matching Gaussian row with stage error at most $C_KBL\log(eq)$ and bad probability at most $C_Kq e^{-c_KL}$.

Pad the initial length $m$ to dyadic $q<2m$ by independent $N_d(0,I_d)$ entries; for $m=1$ take $q=1$. These added laws have empty atom sums and preserve all covariance bounds. Begin with its matching independent Gaussian row. At an active length at least $2q_0$, apply steps 2.1–3.2, taking the target laws to be the designated raw laws in even slots and matching Gaussians in odd slots. Use the root and residual primitives computed from the already realized active Gaussian row, and fresh target terminal kernels. Freeze the newly raw even positions and retain the odd Gaussian positions in their compressed order. Their covariance matrices still lie between $I$ and $KI$. The target product law and [F7] preserve independence of the active row from its frozen complement. At an active length below $2q_0$, independently replace all remaining Gaussian positions by their designated raw laws, using step 3.3, and stop. This constructs the full intended independent raw row after at most $C\log(eN)$ stages, without changing the original Gaussian row.

Every original prefix meets the active positions of each stage in an initial compressed prefix. Triangle inequality adds the stage maximum errors, each at most $C_KBL\log(eN)$, to give total error at most $C_{A,K}B\log^3(eN)$. Always use the ambient $L=a\log(eN)$, even for short compressed rows. The union bad probability is at most $C_KN\log(eN)e^{-c_Ka\log(eN)}$. Choose $a$ sufficiently large depending only on $A,K$ to make this at most $N^{-A}$ for all $N\ge1$; then restrict to the first $m$ entries. This proves the numerical assertion.

For the parameter assertion, every entry law is a measurable kernel obtained by applying addition to the finite product of its supplied atom and Gaussian kernels, using [F5]. Covariance entries are measurable integrals. In dimensions one and two positive definite inverse square roots are continuous functions of their matrices: in dimension two, for $C>0$, $C^{1/2}=(C+\sqrt{\det C}\,I)/\sqrt{\operatorname{tr}C+2\sqrt{\det C}}$, as verified in an eigenbasis by [F3]; the semidefinite zero case is defined by zero and the formula extends continuously. Thus the Gaussian starts and all transforms in steps 1.2–1.3 depend measurably on the parameter. Mixed transformed joint and prefix densities are Gaussian convolution integrals of their raw product kernels, so are jointly measurable by [F5] and strictly positive. Their conditional CDFs are measurable density-ratio integrals. The coordinate quantiles in [F2] are measurable rational infima of those CDFs; hence its root and residual maps are jointly measurable in the parameter and all spatial inputs. The terminal posterior in step 2.2 is likewise a measurable kernel with positive measurable denominator, followed by the explicit Gaussian bridge kernel. Finite kernel products and successive extensions preserve measurability: for one extension define its law by integrating the next kernel against the preceding law; [F5] gives measurable evaluations and [F6] gives countable additivity by monotone convergence of disjoint indicator sums. Iterating this finite construction gives a coupling kernel $Q_\theta$, and every previous marginal and probability bound holds at each parameter. No pointwise selection of conditional-law versions or coupling laws is used.

The integer lengths m<=N, K=1, and weak covariance/atom bounds are included. Constants are chosen before the union bound and uniformly cover all finite N.

subjects.source_mathematical_body_exact:
## Statement

Assume AC. Let $1\le d\le2$, let $(E,\mathcal E)$ be standard Borel, and let $(U_i)_{i\ge0}$ be iid $E$-valued random elements with law $\nu$. Let $h:E^2\to\mathbb R^d$ be measurable with
$$\mathbb E h(U_0,U_1)=0,\qquad \mathbb E|h(U_0,U_1)|^q<\infty$$
for some finite $q>2$. Put $X_i=h(U_i,U_{i+1})$, and define
$$\Gamma=\mathbb E[X_0X_0^T]+\mathbb E[X_0X_1^T]+\mathbb E[X_1X_0^T].$$
Then $\Gamma$ is positive semidefinite. For every fixed $2<p<q$, on an extension preserving the entire original process there are independent centered Gaussian vectors $G_i$ with covariance $\Gamma$ such that
$$\max_{1\le k\le n}\left|\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}(X_i-G_i)\right|=o(n^{1/p})\qquad\hbox{almost surely}.$$
The extension can also carry a standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion $B$ with $\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}G_i=\Gamma^{1/2}B(k)$ for every integer $k\ge0$. Singular $\Gamma$, including $\Gamma=0$, is allowed. Neither the Gaussian row nor $B$ is required to be independent of the original process.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC, the standard-Borel innovation space, the iid sequence $U$, the centered measurable $h$ with its finite $q$th moment, and $2<p<q$. All vector norms are Euclidean and matrix inequalities are quadratic-form inequalities.

[A1] AC supplies the inherited Gaussian, disintegration and countable-extension choices. ([[def-axiom-of-choice]])

[F1] In dimension at most two, independent entries that are finite sums of independent centered atoms bounded by $B\ge1$, plus an independent Gaussian, and whose covariance matrices lie between $I$ and $KI$, admit a uniform $C_{A,K}B\log^3(eN)$ Gaussian coupling with failure at most $N^{-A}$ for a row of length at most $N$. The coupling is a measurable kernel in a supplied standard-Borel environment. ([[lem-heterogeneous-bounded-atom-vector-log-cubed-gaussian-coupling]])

[F2] Independent centered vectors of dimension at most two, covariance $I$ and norm at most $R\ge1$, admit a Gaussian coupling of maximum partial-sum error $C_A R\log^3(eN)$ with failure at most $N^{-A}$, uniformly over all row laws. An existing raw realization can be preserved. ([[lem-bounded-vector-log-cubed-gaussian-coupling]])

[F3] Bounded independent centered real sums satisfy Bernstein's inequality with variance sum $v$ and atom bound $b$: their two-sided tail at $t>0$ is at most $2\exp[-t^2/(2(v+bt/3))]$, with zero sum when $v=0$. ([[thm-bernstein-independent-sums]])

[F4] Conditional Jensen and Cauchy–Schwarz bound the moments and products below; Tonelli and Fubini allow the indicated nonnegative and absolutely integrable iterated expectations. ([[thm-conditional-jensen-inequality]], [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-for-random-variables]], [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]], [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]])

[F5] Real symmetric matrices have orthonormal eigenbases. Gaussian characteristic functions specify their covariances; independent Gaussian vectors form jointly Gaussian stacks, and uncorrelated jointly Gaussian blocks are independent. Standard-normal tails obey $\Pr(|Z|>t)\le2e^{-t^2/2}$ for $t\ge1$. ([[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]], [[lem-characteristic-function-of-a-multivariate-normal-law]], [[lem-finite-independent-gaussian-vectors-form-joint-multivariate-normal]], [[lem-uncorrelated-jointly-gaussian-blocks-are-independent]], [[lem-two-sided-mills-bounds-for-standard-normal-tail]])

[F6] Standard-Borel spaces and their finite products admit disintegration of joint laws; finite Euclidean spaces are standard Borel. Kernel integrals and finite kernel products are measurable. Successive supplied kernels admit a countable extension preserving the initial probability space. ([[def-standard-borel-space]], [[lem-finite-products-of-standard-borel-spaces-are-standard-borel]], [[lem-finite-euclidean-space-is-standard-borel]], [[thm-disintegration-of-a-joint-law-on-standard-borel-spaces]], [[thm-measurability-of-integration-against-a-kernel]], [[lem-finite-products-of-probability-kernels]], [[thm-ionescu-tulcea-construction-of-a-markov-chain]])

[F7] Markov's inequality and the finite union bound control exceptional events; summable exceptional probabilities occur only finitely often almost surely. ([[cor-markov-inequality-for-random-variables]], [[thm-finite-union-bound]], [[thm-first-borel-cantelli]])

[F8] Independent Brownian copies and countable products exist under AC; continuous centered Gaussian paths with the Brownian covariance and independent coordinate increments give standard vector Brownian motion. ([[cor-existence-and-scaling-of-d-dimensional-brownian-motion]], [[thm-countable-product-of-probability-spaces]], [[def-d-dimensional-brownian-motion]])

[F9] Variance and covariance are centered square and product moments. ([[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]])

## Proof

1.1 Write $a(x)=\int h(x,y)\nu(dy)$, $b(y)=\int h(x,y)\nu(dx)$ and $c(x,y)=h(x,y)-a(x)-b(y)$, defining them arbitrarily on the null sets where the integrals are not finite. By [F4], they are measurable, have finite $q$th moments, are centered, and $\mathbb E[c(U,V)\mid U]=\mathbb E[c(U,V)\mid V]=0$ for independent $U,V$ of law $\nu$. Expanding the products using these two zero conditional means gives
$$\Gamma=\operatorname{cov}(a(U)+b(U))+\operatorname{cov}(c(U,V))\ge0.$$
Indeed the variance of $h(U,V)$ is the sum of the covariances of $a(U)$, $b(V)$ and $c(U,V)$, while the lag-one covariance is $\mathbb E[b(U)a(U)^T]$. This proves both the displayed identity and nonnegativity without any limit theorem. [F4, F9, given, construct, algebra]

1.2 For a deterministic orthonormal basis of $\ker\Gamma$, step 1.1's sum of nonnegative scalar variances implies that each basis component of $c$ is zero almost surely and the same component of $a+b$ is zero almost surely. Hence the kernel projection of $h(U_i,U_{i+1})$ is $a_0(U_i)-a_0(U_{i+1})$, where $a_0$ is the kernel projection of $a$. It is an exact endpoint coboundary simultaneously for all $i$, after removing a countable union of null sets. Its partial sums are $a_0(U_0)-a_0(U_k)$. For every $\epsilon>0$, the union and Markov bounds over $k\le2^j$ give probability at most $C\epsilon^{-q}2^{j(1-q/p)}$ that their maximum exceeds $\epsilon2^{j/p}$. This is summable, so [F7], first for rational $\epsilon>0$ and then for all $n$ between successive powers of two, gives maximum $o(n^{1/p})$. If $\Gamma=0$ take $G_i=0$ and adjoin a Brownian motion by [F8]. Otherwise work in its deterministic positive-covariance range of dimension one or two and later restore this kernel projection. [F4, F5, F7, F8, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

1.3 For independent anchors $A,B$ and interior variables $V,W$, all of law $\nu$, put $Y=h(A,V)-a(A)+h(V,W)+h(W,B)-b(B)$. Its conditional mean given $A,B$ is zero. Its average conditional covariance is
$$\Gamma_*:=\mathbb E\operatorname{cov}(Y\mid A,B)=2\operatorname{cov}(a(U)+b(U))+3\operatorname{cov}(c(U,V)).$$
To check this, substitute the decomposition from step 1.1 to write $Y=(a+b)(V)+(a+b)(W)+c(A,V)+c(V,W)+c(W,B)$. Every cross product vanishes after integrating an endpoint using the zero conditional means of $c$; the five individual covariance contributions give the formula. Thus $2\Gamma\le\Gamma_*\le3\Gamma$, so $\Gamma_*$ is positive definite on the range retained in step 1.2. A fixed invertible linear map there makes $\Gamma_*=I$; its inverse will be restored at the end, and all subsequent constants may depend on this fixed map. [F4, F5, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

2.1 Choose fixed $p<\beta<\alpha<q$, and consider an epoch of $N=2^j$ consecutive triple indices. Put $R=N^{1/\alpha}$, $L=K\log(eN)$ and $m=\lceil R^2L\rceil$. In this epoch replace the normalized active $h$ by $f=h\mathbf1_{\{|h|\le R\}}-\mathbb E[h\mathbf1_{\{|h|\le R\}}]$. Then $|f|\le2R$, $\mathbb E|f|^q\le C$, and its means $a_R,b_R$ and degenerate component $c_R$ have uniformly bounded $q$th moments by [F4]. They converge in $L^2$ to their untruncated versions: the squared tail is at most $R^{2-q}\mathbb E|h|^q$, and conditional averaging is an $L^2$ contraction by coordinatewise [F4]. Consequently the average conditional triple-noise covariance $\Gamma_{*,R}=2\operatorname{cov}(a_R+b_R)+3\operatorname{cov}(c_R)$ tends to $I$. For all sufficiently large deterministic epochs, $c_0I\le\Gamma_{*,R}\le C_0I$ for fixed $c_0,C_0>0$. Finitely many earlier epochs can be coupled arbitrarily and contribute only finite errors. [F4, F5, step 1.3, given, construct, choose, algebra]

2.2 Let $A_t=U_{3t}$, $V_t=U_{3t+1}$ and $W_t=U_{3t+2}$ in the epoch, relabeling its first triple index as zero. Conditional on its anchors $(A_0,\ldots,A_N)$, the interior pairs $(V_t,W_t)$ are independent, and the centered triple noises
$$Y_t=f(A_t,V_t)-a_R(A_t)+f(V_t,W_t)+f(W_t,A_{t+1})-b_R(A_{t+1})$$
are independent centered vectors bounded by $CR$. Define the symmetric matrices $Q(z)=\operatorname{cov}(f(V,W)+f(W,z)-b_R(z))$ and $P(z)=\operatorname{cov}(f(z,V)-a_R(z))+\operatorname{cov}(f(z,V),f(V,W))+\operatorname{cov}(f(V,W),f(z,V))$, where these covariances integrate independent $V,W$. The left and right endpoint terms are independent given the anchors, so
$$V_t:=\operatorname{cov}(Y_t\mid A_t,A_{t+1})=P(A_t)+Q(A_{t+1}),\qquad D_t:=P(A_t)+Q(A_t)=\operatorname{cov}(Y(A_t,A_t)\mid A_t).$$
Although $P$ need not be positive semidefinite, $V_t,D_t,Q(A_t)$ are positive semidefinite, their norms are at most $CR^2$, and $\mathbb EV_t=\mathbb ED_t=\Gamma_{*,R}$. Moreover, for every interval of triple indices,
$$\sum_{t=u}^{v-1}(V_t-D_t)=Q(A_v)-Q(A_u).$$
These are identities of measurable anchor functions, by [F4] and [F6]. [F4, F6, F9, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

2.3 Divide the epoch into consecutive chunks of length $m$, leaving a shorter final chunk. The entries of $V_t$ are one-dependent functions of adjacent iid anchors, while $D_t$ are iid functions of individual anchors. For a positive semidefinite matrix $T$ of norm at most $CR^2$, $|T_{uv}|^2\le T_{uu}T_{vv}\le CR^2T_{uu}$. Its entrywise second moments here are therefore at most $CR^2$, because the mean matrices in step 2.2 are uniformly bounded. Within each parity the entries of $V_t$ are independent. Apply [F3] separately to both parities and each matrix entry, and to the independent entries of $D_t$ across $t$. For any full chunk $I$, the probability that an entry of either centered covariance sum exceeds a fixed small multiple of $m$ is at most $C\exp(-cm/R^2)$. Since $\|T\|_{\rm op}\le d\max_{u,v}|T_{uv}|$ for symmetric matrices in dimension $d\le2$, choose the multiplier small relative to $c_0$ and union over at most $N$ chunks and their entries. Choosing $K$ sufficiently large gives an anchor event of probability at least $1-N^{-A}$, for any prescribed $A>0$, on which
$$c_1mI\le\sum_{t\in I}V_t\le C_1mI,\qquad c_1mI\le\sum_{t\in I}D_t\le C_1mI$$
for every full chunk, with both sums bounded on both sides. The same entrywise Bernstein calculation gives an upper bound $C_1mI$ on both sums in the shorter chunk. Here and below the constants may be enlarged independently of $N$ and $R$. Since $\alpha>2$, $m<N$ eventually; if not, the same upper bound handles the entire epoch as one residual chunk. [F3, F5, F7, step 2.1, step 2.2, choose, algebra]

2.4 On a good anchor vector, divide each full-chunk sum of $Y_t$ by $\sqrt{c_1m}$. Its conditional covariance lies between $I$ and $KI$, for a fixed $K$, and it is a sum of independent centered atoms of norm at most $CR/\sqrt m\le C$. Its whole value need not be bounded. Its atom kernels are the measurable pushforwards of $\nu\otimes\nu$ under the formula in step 2.2; independence holds conditional on the supplied anchors. Thus [F1], with the ambient length parameter $N$ and a fixed atom bound $B\ge\max(1,C)$, supplies a measurable coupling of the chunk sums with independent matching Gaussian chunk sums. Undoing the normalization gives maximum chunk-boundary error at most $C\sqrt m\log^3(eN)\le CR\log^{7/2}(eN)$, with conditional failure at most $N^{-A}$. On bad anchors use independent product coupling instead, preserving both marginals. No theorem about uniformly bounded grouped values is being invoked. [A1, F1, F6, step 2.2, step 2.3, construct, algebra]

2.5 Fill a Gaussian chunk of total covariance $S>0$ and coupled sum $z$ with increments of individual covariances $V_t$ by taking independent $H_t\sim N(0,V_t)$ and setting $H'_t=H_t+V_tS^{-1}(z-\sum H_t)$. The residual $H_t-V_tS^{-1}\sum H_t$ is independent of the original total Gaussian by [F5]; direct covariance calculation shows this is its exact conditional bridge law and its sum is $z$. Thus the completed Gaussian noise row has exactly its conditional independent Gaussian product law. Conditional on good anchors, every within-chunk raw prefix has atom bound $CR$ and covariance at most $C_1mI$. Coordinatewise [F3] and Gaussian tails in [F5], with a union bound over at most $N$ prefixes, bound both raw and Gaussian within-chunk norms by $C(\sqrt{mL}+RL)\le CRL$, with failure at most $N^{-A}$ after enlarging $K$. Couple a shorter residual chunk independently and use its covariance upper bound in the same calculation. Consequently there is a conditional noise-row coupling $Y_t\leftrightarrow Z_t^V$, with $Z_t^V$ conditionally independent $N(0,V_t)$, of full-prefix error $CR\log^{7/2}(eN)$ and total failure $CN^{-A}$. Its extension to the actually given $Y_t$ follows by [F6] disintegrating the finite joint law given anchors and $Y_t$; the original innovations are preserved. [F3, F5, F6, F7, step 2.3, step 2.4, construct, algebra]

3.1 To redistribute covariance without a matrix random clock, start instead with independent standard Gaussian vectors $Z_t$, independent of the anchors, and put $Z_t^D=D_t^{1/2}Z_t$. These have the required conditional independent $D_t$ row law even if individual $D_t$ are singular. On good anchors group them into the same full chunks, whose covariances $B_i=\sum D_t$ are positive definite. Write $A_i=\sum V_t$ for the desired other row. Pad to a dyadic number of chunks with independent identical-covariance $mI$ Gaussian entries in both rows. All chunk covariances lie between $c_1mI$ and $C_1mI$, and every contiguous whole-chunk interval satisfies $\|A_I-B_I\|\le CR^2$ by step 2.2's endpoint identity; padded intervals retain that bound. We construct the $A$ row from the already given $B$ row using the Gaussian tree in the next two steps, leaving the original $Z_t$ unchanged. [F5, step 2.2, step 2.3, construct, algebra]

3.2 At a node of $s$ chunks and for either covariance row $C$, write $C_P=C_L+C_R$, $H_C=C_LC_P^{-1}$, and $T_C=C_L-C_LC_P^{-1}C_L=(C_L^{-1}+C_R^{-1})^{-1}$. Thus $C_P$ and $T_C$ have eigenvalues comparable to $sm$, and the Gaussian parent and residual $S_L-H_CS_P$ are independent by [F5]. Extract their standardized independent Gaussian primitives from the given $B$ row, and use the same primitives to construct the $A$ root and residuals. For positive definite matrices $M,N$, the identity $M^{1/2}X+XN^{1/2}=M-N$, with $X=M^{1/2}-N^{1/2}$, yields $\|X\|\le C\|M-N\|/(\sqrt{\lambda_{\min}M}+\sqrt{\lambda_{\min}N})$: solve it by integrating $e^{-tM^{1/2}}(M-N)e^{-tN^{1/2}}$ and bound the integral. The endpoint bounds in step 3.1 and the inverse identity imply $\|H_A-H_B\|\le CR^2/(sm)$, $\|T_A-T_B\|\le CR^2$, and $\|T_A^{1/2}-T_B^{1/2}\|\le CR^2/\sqrt{sm}$. A union bound over the Gaussian parents and primitives gives, outside probability $N^{-A}$, $|S_P^B|\le C\sqrt{smL}$ and primitive norms at most $C\sqrt L$. Reconstruct children by $S_L^C=H_CS_P^C+T_C^{1/2}z_I$ and $S_R^C=S_P^C-S_L^C$. Their errors satisfy $e_L=H_Ae_P+\eta_I$, $e_R=(I-H_A)e_P-\eta_I$, with $|\eta_I|\le CR^2\sqrt{L/(sm)}\le CR$, and the root error is also at most $CR$. Every child and root marginal is its exact Gaussian law, so the two completed chunk rows each have their required conditional product law. [F5, F7, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

3.3 The prefix bound uses exact covariance interpolation, not repeated norm bounds on $H_A$. In any subtree its leading root coefficient is $A_{\mathrm{prefix}}A_P^{-1}$. At a boundary ancestor its residual coefficient is $A_{\mathrm{partial\ left}}A_L^{-1}$ if the boundary is in the left child, and $I-A_{\mathrm{partial\ right}}A_R^{-1}$ if it is in the right child. For the left case substitute the child's leading term and cancel $A_L^{-1}A_L$; for the right case add the full left error to the partial right error, giving leading coefficient $(A_L+A_{\mathrm{partial\ right}})A_P^{-1}$ and the stated residual coefficient. This proves the expansion by induction. Each coefficient has norm at most $1+C_1/c_1$, using the count and eigenvalue bounds on chunk covariances, and there are at most $C\log(eN)$ boundary ancestors. Step 3.2 therefore gives prefix error $CR\log(eN)$ at chunk boundaries. Fill the $V_t$ Gaussian increments by the bridge in step 2.5; the $D_t$ increments were already present. Their within-chunk prefix norms are at most $C\sqrt{mL}\le CRL$ by Gaussian tails and the covariance upper bounds. Handle a short residual chunk independently. This gives full-prefix Gaussian-row error $CR\log(eN)$ outside probability $CN^{-A}$. On bad anchors use an independent $V_t$ row while retaining the original independent standard $Z_t$. All operations are measurable matrix functions and finite Gaussian kernels. [F5, F6, F7, step 2.3, step 2.5, step 3.1, step 3.2, algebra]

3.4 The couplings of steps 2.5 and 3.3 have the same joint anchor and $V_t$-Gaussian-row marginal. Disintegrate the second joint law to give its standard $Z$ row conditional on that common anchor and Gaussian row, and append it to the first coupling. The disintegration formula in [F6] proves that both joint laws, hence both error estimates, are preserved. In particular the original innovations remain unchanged and the $Z_t$ row is still independent standard Gaussian conditional on anchors. The two full-prefix errors add. Adding back the conditional means of the triples now gives an iid replacement row
$$L_t=D_t^{1/2}Z_t+a_R(A_t)+b_R(A_t),$$
since the pairs $(A_t,Z_t)$ are iid. Indeed the original mean sum is $\sum_{t<k}(a_R(A_t)+b_R(A_{t+1}))=\sum_{t<k}(a_R(A_t)+b_R(A_t))+b_R(A_k)-b_R(A_0)$. The endpoint means have uniformly bounded $q$th moments by step 2.1. Their maximum exceeds $R$ with probability at most $CN R^{-q}$ by [F7]. Therefore the original truncated triple sums and the partial sums of $L_t$ have maximum error $CR\log^{7/2}(eN)$ with failure at most $CN^{-A}+CN R^{-q}$. [F4, F6, F7, step 2.1, step 2.5, step 3.3, construct, algebra]

3.5 The row $L_t$ is centered and has uniformly bounded $q$th moment: conditional Gaussian moments and coordinatewise [F4] give $\mathbb E\|D_t\|^{q/2}\le C\mathbb E|Y(A_t,A_t)|^q\le C\mathbb E|f(U,V)|^q\le C$, and the mean terms satisfy the same bound. Write $\gamma_0=\mathbb E[f(U_0,U_1)f(U_0,U_1)^T]$, $\gamma_1=\mathbb E[f(U_0,U_1)f(U_1,U_2)^T]$, and $\Gamma_R=\gamma_0+\gamma_1+\gamma_1^T$. The variance of a triple is $3\gamma_0+2(\gamma_1+\gamma_1^T)$. Subtracting the covariance of its conditional mean $a_R(A_0)+b_R(A_1)$ gives $\mathbb ED_t$ by total variance. Since $\mathbb E[b_R(U)a_R(U)^T]=\gamma_1$, adding $\operatorname{cov}(a_R+b_R)$ gives
$$\operatorname{cov}(L_t)=3\Gamma_R.$$
This is a direct finite product calculation, independent of convergence in law or an inference from a coupling error. As $R\to\infty$, $\Gamma_R\to\Gamma$, which is positive definite in the active space; hence these iid covariances have fixed upper and positive lower eigenvalue bounds in every sufficiently large epoch. [F4, F5, F9, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 3.4, algebra]

4.1 We derive the finite-horizon iid bound needed for this changing row directly from [F2]. Suppose $T_1,\ldots,T_N$ are iid centered vectors with $\mathbb E|T_1|^q\le M$, and covariance $\Sigma$ whose eigenvalues lie in a fixed $[\lambda,\Lambda]$ with $\lambda>0$. Put $R_2=N^{1/\beta}$ and $T'_i=T_i\mathbf1_{\{|T_i|\le R_2\}}-\mu$, $\mu=\mathbb E[T_1\mathbf1_{\{|T_1|\le R_2\}}]$. The tail union probability is at most $MN R_2^{-q}$, and on its complement the maximum sum correction is at most $MN R_2^{1-q}=O(R_2)$. Also $\Sigma-\Sigma'=\mathbb E[T_1T_1^T\mathbf1_{\{|T_1|>R_2\}}]+\mu\mu^T$, so $\|\Sigma-\Sigma'\|\le C_MR_2^{2-q}$. Uniformly for all sufficiently large $N$ the eigenvalues of $\Sigma'$ are in $[\lambda/2,C]$. The whitened $T'_i$ have covariance $I$ and norm at most $CR_2$, so [F2] yields independent standard $H_i$ with maximum coupling error to $\Sigma'^{1/2}H_i$ at most $C R_2\log^3(eN)$, outside probability $N^{-A}$. All constants are uniform in the iid law under these moment and eigenvalue bounds. [F2, F5, F7, construct, algebra]

4.2 Step 3.2's square-root bound gives $\|\Sigma^{1/2}-\Sigma'^{1/2}\|\le C_MR_2^{2-q}$. Use the same $H_i$ and apply Gaussian tails to all its partial sums to bound the covariance correction by $C_M\sqrt N R_2^{2-q}\sqrt{\log(eN)}$ with failure at most $N^{-A}$. This is $o(R_2)$ because $\beta<q<2(q-1)$. Consequently steps 4.1 and 4.2 give a finite-row iid coupling with matching covariance $\Sigma$, error $C R_2\log^3(eN)$ and failure $CN^{-A}+MN R_2^{-q}$. Apply this result to the varying laws $T_i=L_i$ from step 3.5, using their uniform moment and eigenvalue bounds. This uses no fixed-law asymptotic iid theorem and asserts no triangular-law interface absent from a supplier's Statement. [F5, F7, step 3.2, step 3.5, step 4.1, algebra]

5.1 The original normalized active $h$ and $f$ agree up to their global mean correction unless one of the epoch's $3N$ observations exceeds $R$, an event of probability at most $CN R^{-q}$. The mean correction is at most $CN R^{1-q}=O(R)$. Moreover $\|\Gamma_R-\Gamma\|\le CR^{2-q}$. For the lag-one product difference, use $|h_0h_1^T-f_0f_1^T|\le C(|h_0|+|h_1|)^2\mathbf1_{\{|h_0|+|h_1|>R\}}$ before centering and then include the mean correction. Pointwise the displayed squared tail is at most a constant times the sum of the squared tails of $|h_0|$ and $|h_1|$ above $R/2$, so its expectation is at most $CR^{2-q}\mathbb E|h|^q$. The variance term has the same bound. Since $\Gamma$ is positive definite in the active space, couple the iid Gaussian triple increments of covariance $3\Gamma_R$ from step 4.2 to increments of covariance $3\Gamma$ using the same standard normals. Step 3.2's square-root bound and Gaussian tails make the maximum correction at most $C\sqrt N R^{2-q}\sqrt{\log(eN)}=o(R)$ with failure $N^{-A}$, because $\alpha<q<2(q-1)$. Thus each sufficiently large epoch of original triple sums can be coupled to independent Gaussian increments of covariance $3\Gamma$, with error $C N^{1/\beta}\log^{7/2}(eN)$ and failure at most
$$C N^{-A}+C N^{1-q/\alpha}+C N^{1-q/\beta}.$$
Here $R=N^{1/\alpha}\le N^{1/\beta}$, and all constants are uniform over epochs. [F4, F5, F7, step 2.1, step 3.2, step 3.4, step 3.5, step 4.2, algebra]

5.2 Retain triple index $t=0$ as a finite initial prefix, coupled arbitrarily, and perform the finite constructions on epochs $\{2^j,\ldots,2^{j+1}-1\}$ of triple indices, $j\ge0$, using fresh kernels. Each conditional noise coupling and each Gaussian redistribution has the full conditional product marginal given all anchors. Because the original interior pairs are independent conditional on anchors, their finite-epoch kernel products give a product standard $Z$ law conditional on all anchors. Hence the pairs $(A_t,Z_t)$, and therefore the replacement variables $L_t$ with the deterministic epoch-dependent function in step 3.4, are independent across epochs as well as within them. Each later iid-row coupling is glued through its finite replacement row by [F6]; because these rows are independent, products of their kernels give independent final Gaussian rows across epochs. These statements follow by integrating finite rectangles under the conditional product laws, so no independence is being inferred from an error bound. All anchor sets and row coordinates involved in an epoch are finite standard-Borel products, making these disintegrations legitimate. Apply [F6]'s countable kernel extension with the entire original probability space as its initial coordinate to preserve all original innovations. The failure bounds in step 5.1 are summable over $N=2^j$, since $\beta<\alpha<q$. By [F7], all sufficiently large epochs satisfy their error bounds almost surely; finitely many earlier errors can be included in a finite random constant. [A1, F6, F7, step 2.2, step 2.5, step 3.1, step 3.4, step 4.2, step 5.1, construct, algebra]

5.3 Sum the completed epoch errors and the current partial one. The geometric bound $\sum_{j\le J}2^{j/\beta}(j+1)^{7/2}\le C_\beta2^{J/\beta}(J+1)^{7/2}$ gives a global triple-prefix error $O(n^{1/\beta}\log^{7/2}(en))=o(n^{1/p})$. Map back from the fixed normalization in step 1.3 and restore the covariance-kernel coboundary from step 1.2. Split each independent Gaussian triple increment $H_t\sim N(0,3\Gamma)$ into three increments of covariance $\Gamma$: for each $t$ take a fresh triple $K_{t,0},K_{t,1},K_{t,2}\sim N(0,\Gamma)$, independent across all $t,r$ and of all triple increments, and put $G_{3t+r}=H_t/3+K_{t,r}-(K_{t,0}+K_{t,1}+K_{t,2})/3$. By [F5] these three increments are jointly Gaussian, each has covariance $\Gamma$ and distinct ones have zero cross covariance, so the entire resulting row is independent with covariance $\Gamma$. At nontriple endpoints the original sum changes by at most two $X_i$, and the Gaussian sum by at most two $G_i$. Union and Markov bounds on dyadic ranges, using respectively their finite $q$th moments and arbitrary Gaussian moments, show both maxima are $o(n^{1/p})$, as in step 1.2. This proves the stated full-prefix approximation. [F5, F7, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 5.1, step 5.2, construct, algebra]

5.4 In a fixed orthonormal eigenbasis of $\Gamma$, divide each positive-variance Gaussian coordinate by its fixed standard deviation and add independent standard Gaussian coordinates in the zero-variance directions. This yields independent standard normal vector increments realizing $G_i$ by $\Gamma^{1/2}$. For each integer interval adjoin independent Brownian copies by [F8] and use their bridges $W(t)-tW(1)$, independently of the existing increments. Interpolate the standard Gaussian random walk linearly on that interval plus its bridge. The paths are continuous and direct covariance calculation gives $\min(s,t)I_d$; finite Gaussianity and zero cross covariances give independent normal increments by [F5]. Thus [F8] identifies a standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion, and the fixed eigenbasis map gives $\sum_{i<k}G_i=\Gamma^{1/2}B(k)$ at every integer $k$. This construction also applies when $\Gamma=0$ by adjoining an independent Brownian motion. It does not alter the original-process marginal or any error already proved. [A1, F5, F8, step 1.2, step 5.3, construct, algebra] ∎

## Source notes

The conditional triple decomposition follows the finite-memory mechanism in Berkes–Liu–Wu. Every coupling theorem used as a premise is proved locally. The first coupling uses independent bounded atoms in a random environment, the covariance redistribution is a direct Gaussian matrix tree, and the changing iid replacement laws are handled by the explicit finite-horizon argument in steps 4.1–4.2. No independent-nonidentical strong approximation, matrix random clock, or uniform triangular-law asymptotic theorem is imported.

manifest_row.statement:
Assume AC. Let $1\le d\le2$, let $(E,\mathcal E)$ be standard Borel, and let $(U_i)_{i\ge0}$ be iid $E$-valued random elements with law $\nu$. Let $h:E^2\to\mathbb R^d$ be measurable with
$$\mathbb E h(U_0,U_1)=0,\qquad \mathbb E|h(U_0,U_1)|^q<\infty$$
for some finite $q>2$. Put $X_i=h(U_i,U_{i+1})$, and define
$$\Gamma=\mathbb E[X_0X_0^T]+\mathbb E[X_0X_1^T]+\mathbb E[X_1X_0^T].$$
Then $\Gamma$ is positive semidefinite. For every fixed $2<p<q$, on an extension preserving the entire original process there are independent centered Gaussian vectors $G_i$ with covariance $\Gamma$ such that
$$\max_{1\le k\le n}\left|\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}(X_i-G_i)\right|=o(n^{1/p})\qquad\hbox{almost surely}.$$
The extension can also carry a standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion $B$ with $\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}G_i=\Gamma^{1/2}B(k)$ for every integer $k\ge0$. Singular $\Gamma$, including $\Gamma=0$, is allowed. Neither the Gaussian row nor $B$ is required to be independent of the original process.
