citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Fix $0<\gamma\le1$. Let $1\le d\le4$, $s>0$, $B>0$, and let $X_1,\ldots,X_m,Z$ be independent centered random vectors in $\mathbb R^d$, where $m\ge0$, $|X_j|\le B$ almost surely, and $Z\sim N_d(0,G)$. Suppose $S=Z+\sum_jX_j$ has covariance $sI_d$ and $G\ge\gamma sI_d$ in quadratic form order. There is an absolute constant $C_0\ge1$ such that, with $\tau=C_0B$, the logarithmic moment generating function
$$K(z)=\log\mathbb E e^{z\cdot S},\qquad K(0)=0,$$
has a single analytic branch on the complex Euclidean ball $\tau|z|<1$, and
$$|\partial_u\partial_v^2K(z)|\le\tau s|u||v|^2\qquad(u,v\in\mathbb R^d,\ \tau|z|<1).$$
Here $z\cdot S$ uses the complex bilinear dot product and $|z|^2=\sum_i|z_i|^2$. Every real exponential tilt $\mathbb P_h(d\omega)=e^{h\cdot S-K(h)}\mathbb P(d\omega)$ is defined, and its characteristic function satisfies
$$|\varphi_h(t)|:=|\mathbb E_h e^{it\cdot S}|\le e^{-\gamma s|t|^2/2}\qquad(t,h\in\mathbb R^d),$$
where $K(h)=\log\mathbb E e^{h\cdot S}$ for real $h$, also outside the analytic ball. Put $\kappa=\tau/\sqrt s$. For every fixed $a>0$ and integer $N\ge1$ there is a finite $C_{a,N,\gamma}$, uniform in $1\le d\le4$, such that, if $0<\kappa\le1$,
$$(2\pi)^{-d}\int_{|t|\ge a/\tau}|\varphi_h(t)|\,dt\le C_{a,N,\gamma}\kappa^Ns^{-d/2},$$
$$(2\pi)^{-d}\int_{|t|\ge a/\tau}|t\cdot v||\varphi_h(t)|\,dt\le C_{a,N,\gamma}\kappa^N|v|s^{-(d+1)/2}.$$
All assertions hold with the same $C_0$, $B$, $s$, and $\gamma$ for $AS$, where $A$ is any real $k\times d$ matrix with $1\le k\le d$ and $AA^T=I_k$. This includes every coordinate prefix, every orthogonal change of coordinates, and their compositions. In particular it covers the normalized joint sum and difference of two independent children by applying the assertion in their joint dimension, provided that dimension is at most four and the joint input satisfies the stated covariance assumptions.

Assume AC and the hypotheses of [[lem-gaussian-anchored-sums-have-cumulant-and-fourier-bounds]]: $S=Z+\sum_{i=1}^mX_i\in\mathbb R^d$, $1\le d\le4$, the centered summands are independent, $|X_i|\le B$, $Z$ is Gaussian with covariance $G\ge\gamma sI_d$, and $\operatorname{cov}(S)=sI_d$, where $s,B>0$ and $0<\gamma\le1$. Put $\tau=C_0B$, with $C_0$ from that supplier, and let $\Phi_s$ be the CDF of $N(0,s)$. There are constants $c_\gamma>0$ and $C_\gamma<\infty$, independent of the summand laws, $m,d,s,B$, with the following properties.

For $1\le j\le d$, let $H_j(x',y)$ be the conditional CDF of $S_j$ given $S_{<j}=x'\in\mathbb R^{j-1}$ obtained by dividing the joint prefix density by its marginal density. These densities are strictly positive, so this defines a probability kernel at every $x'$, including prefixes of probability zero. Its quantile transport
$$T_j(x',z)=H_j(x',\cdot)^{-1}(\Phi_s(z))$$
is jointly Borel measurable and takes a fresh $N(0,s)$ variable to that conditional law. If $s\ge C_\gamma\tau^2$, then, with $y=T_j(x',z)$,
$$|y-z|\le C_\gamma\tau\left(1+\frac{|x'|^2+y^2}{s}\right)\quad\hbox{when }|x'|+|y|\le c_\gamma s/\tau,$$
and also
$$|T_j(x',z)-z|\le C_\gamma\tau\left(1+\frac{|x'|^2+z^2}{s}\right)\quad\hbox{when }|x'|+|z|\le c_\gamma s/\tau.$$
For $j=1$, the prefix is empty and its norm is zero. The resulting successive coordinate transport $R$ sends $N_d(0,sI_d)$ to the law of $S$ and satisfies
$$|R(g)-g|\le C_\gamma\tau\left(1+\frac{|R(g)|^2}{s}\right)\quad\hbox{when }|R(g)|\le c_\gamma s/\tau.$$

If $d=2a$ with $a\le2$, write $S=(P,D)$ with $P,D\in\mathbb R^a$. The last $a$ successive conditional transports give a jointly measurable $T_p$ taking a fresh $E\sim N_a(0,sI_a)$ to the conditional law of $D$ given $P=p$, and
$$|T_p(e)-e|\le C_\gamma\tau\left(1+\frac{|p|^2+|T_p(e)|^2}{s}\right)$$
when $s\ge C_\gamma\tau^2$ and $|p|,|T_p(e)|\le c_\gamma s/\tau$. The Gaussian reference bridge $E$ is independent of its Gaussian parent.

There is also the following scalar unequal-variance form. Let $L,R$ be independent centered scalar sums of independent variables bounded by $B$ and independent Gaussian terms, with variances $V_L,V_R\in[s/2,s]$, and with Gaussian component variances at least $\gamma V_L,\gamma V_R$, respectively. Put
$$W=V_L+V_R,\qquad w=V_L/W,\qquad v=V_LV_R/W,\qquad P=L+R,\qquad D=L-wP.$$
Then $W\in[s,2s]$, $w\in[1/3,2/3]$, $v\in[s/4,s/2]$. There is a jointly measurable transport taking a fresh $N(0,v)$ variable to $D$ conditional on $P=p$ with
$$|T_p(e)-e|\le C_\gamma\tau\left(1+\frac{p^2+T_p(e)^2}{s}\right)$$
when $s\ge C_\gamma\tau^2$ and $|p|,|T_p(e)|\le c_\gamma s/\tau$. The corresponding root transport from $N(0,W)$ to $P$ obeys the analogous bound with $|P|^2/s$. The reconstructed children are $L=wP+D$ and $R=(1-w)P-D$.

All these maps are jointly measurable in an additional measurable parameter whenever, on each fixed finite row length, the bounded input laws are probability kernels, their Gaussian covariance and $s$ are measurable functions, and the displayed hypotheses hold parameterwise. This includes countable arrays with different row lengths. No claim here asserts the conditional estimates for raw bounded laws without a positive Gaussian component.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

Assume AC. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then $$\Phi_X(t):=\mathbb E e^{it\cdot X}=\exp(it\cdot m-t^T\Sigma t/2)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R^d).$$ This transform uniquely determines the law, including singular Sigma.

Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$, $m\in\mathbb R^d$, and let $\Sigma$ be a real symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then its law has Lebesgue density
$$f_{m,\Sigma}(x)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}\det(\Sigma)^{-1/2} \exp\!\left(-\tfrac12(x-m)^T\Sigma^{-1}(x-m)\right), \qquad x\in\mathbb R^d.$$

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

Let $(S,\Sigma)$ and $(T_i,\Tau_i)$ for $i<n$ be measurable spaces, with
$n<\infty$, and let $K_i:S\to T_i$ be probability kernels with the same
source. There is a unique probability kernel
$$K:S\to\prod_{i<n}T_i$$
whose evaluation on every measurable rectangle is
$$K(s,\prod_{i<n}B_i)=\prod_{i<n}K_i(s,B_i).$$
For $n=0$, the target is the empty-product singleton and $K$ is its point
mass. For $n>0$, the product sigma-algebra is the recursive finite product
sigma-algebra.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Assume AC. Let $L,R,C,V$ be random elements in arbitrary measurable spaces. Suppose $L\perp\!\!\!\perp R\mid\sigma(C)$ and that the joint law of $(L,R,C,V)$ is obtained from the law of $(L,R,C)$ by a probability kernel $K(l,c,dv)$ depending only on $(l,c)$. Then
$$(L,V)\perp\!\!\!\perp R\mid\sigma(C),\qquad L\perp\!\!\!\perp R\mid\sigma(C,V).$$
No regular conditional law on an unspecified measurable space is assumed: $K$ is supplied in the hypotheses.

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

For every finite family of events $A_0,\ldots,A_{n-1}$,
$$\mathbb P\!\left(\bigcup_{i<n}A_i\right)\le\sum_{i<n}\mathbb P(A_i).$$
For $n=0$ both sides are $0$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Let $n\ge1$, let $X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}$ be independent real random variables on a
common probability space, and let $g_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be Borel
measurable for each $i<n$.

1. If every $g_i$ is nonnegative, then
   $$\mathbb E\left[\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)\right]=\prod_{i<n}\mathbb E[g_i(X_i)]$$
   in $[0,+\infty]$. In this finite product of expectations, a zero factor
   makes the product zero even when another factor is $+\infty$; otherwise
   multiplication has its usual extended nonnegative meaning.
2. If every $g_i(X_i)$ is integrable, then $\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)$ is integrable
   and the same factorization holds in $\mathbb R$.

derivations.claim:
For a coordinate $Y$ of one centered atom, $E|Y|^r\le B^{r-2}EY^2$ for every integer $r\ge2$. Absolute exponential-series integration is legitimate because $\sum_r|hY|^r/r!\le e^{B|h|}$; [F6] permits summing its nonnegative absolute terms, and its positive and negative parts then give the signed series identity. For $B|h|<1$, centering cancels the linear term and $r!\ge2$ for $r\ge2$, so
$$\log Ee^{hY}\le Ee^{hY}-1\le\frac{h^2EY^2}{2(1-B|h|)}.$$
A centered Gaussian coordinate has logarithmic mgf $h^2\operatorname{var}(Z)/2$, by completing the square in its positive-variance eigencoordinates using [F3] and [F4]; zero-variance coordinates vanish. Independence multiplies the finitely many atom and Gaussian mgfs. Since their variances add to each coordinate variance of $X_i$, at most $K$, any sum of $s$ entries, also with arbitrary matching Gaussian replacements, has coordinate log mgf at most $Ks h^2/[2(1-B|h|)]$. For a coordinate threshold $u>0$ use $h=u/(Ks+Bu)$ and exponential Markov for both signs. This gives tail at most $2\exp\{-u^2/[2(Ks+Bu)]\}$. The coordinate union bound therefore gives, uniformly in atom counts,
$$\Pr\!\left(\left|\sum_{i\in I}X_i\right|>C_K[\sqrt{st}+Bt]\right)\le C_K e^{-c_Kt},\qquad t\ge1.$$
This holds for every contiguous interval in any compressed ordering.

Consider a dyadic mixed row whose odd entries are independent matching Gaussians and whose even entries have their raw laws. At a node of $s\ge4$ entries let its two child covariance matrices be $U,V$, put $W=U+V$, and, for its target child sums $S_L,S_R$, define
$$P=S_L+S_R,\qquad H=UW^{-1},\qquad D=S_L-HP,\qquad R=U-UW^{-1}U.$$
Independence gives $\operatorname{cov}(P)=W$, $\operatorname{cov}(P,D)=U-WW^{-1}U=0$, and $\operatorname{cov}(D)=R$. The symmetric matrix $R$ equals $UW^{-1}V$ and has inverse $V^{-1}WU^{-1}=U^{-1}+V^{-1}$; hence it is positive definite without assuming commutation. Since each child has $s/2$ entries, [F3] gives
$$\tfrac s2I\le U,V\le\tfrac{Ks}2I,\qquad sI\le W\le KsI,\qquad \tfrac s4I\le R\le\tfrac{Ks}4I.$$
The final inequalities follow by inverting, adding, and reinverting the quadratic form bounds.

The transformed pair $Q=\sqrt s\operatorname{diag}(W^{-1/2},R^{-1/2})(P,D)$ has covariance $sI_{2d}$. A raw atom $x$ in its left or right child contributes respectively
$$\sqrt s\bigl(W^{-1/2}x,R^{-1/2}VW^{-1}x\bigr),\qquad \sqrt s\bigl(W^{-1/2}x,-R^{-1/2}UW^{-1}x\bigr).$$
Their norms are at most $C_KB$, since $\sqrt s\|W^{-1/2}\|\le1$, $\sqrt s\|R^{-1/2}\|\le2$, and $\|UW^{-1}\|,\|VW^{-1}\|\le K/2$. Each child contains half Gaussian entries, so its Gaussian covariance is at least $(s/4)I$, at least $\gamma$ times its total covariance with $\gamma=1/(2K)$. Congruence of quadratic forms therefore makes the Gaussian covariance of $Q$ at least $\gamma sI_{2d}$. All its bounded contributions are the independently transformed original atoms, and all Gaussian contributions combine into an independent Gaussian. Thus [F1] and [F2] apply directly to $Q$, including its coordinate prefixes. The conditioning is on its first $d$ coordinates. Undoing the separate parent and residual whitening, whose inverse norms are bounded by $C_K$, gives a transport of a fresh $E_I\sim N_d(0,R)$ to $D$ conditional on $P=p$, with error
$$|T_{I,p}(E_I)-E_I|\le C_KB\left(1+\frac{|p|^2+|T_{I,p}(E_I)|^2}{s}\right)$$
when $s\ge C_KB^2$ and the two target norms are at most $c_Ks/B$. The root has the analogous transport from $N_d(0,W)$ with error $C_KB(1+|P|^2/s)$. There is no additional factor from the atom counts or from $\sqrt s$.

Temporarily take a dyadic current length $q\le2N$, set $L=a\log(eN)$, and let $q_0$ be the least dyadic integer at least $H_KB^2L$, with $H_K$ to be fixed. Suppose $q\ge2q_0$. Start with an independent Gaussian row having the individual covariances $D_i$. Its root sum and residuals $E_I=V_L-UW^{-1}V_I$ at the active nodes are mutually independent Gaussian vectors of covariances $W_{\rm root}$ and $R_I$: the cross covariances vanish, and independence follows recursively from [F4]. Apply the root transport in step 1.3 and then, descending the tree, set $D_I=T_{I,S_I}(E_I)$ and
$$S_L=UW^{-1}S_I+D_I,\quad S_R=VW^{-1}S_I-D_I,\quad V_L=UW^{-1}V_I+E_I,\quad V_R=VW^{-1}V_I-E_I.$$
Stop at length $q_0$. Each fresh residual is independent of the already exposed parents, so every target split has exactly its prescribed conditional law. For Gaussians the child covariance is $UW^{-1}U+R=U$ and the cross covariance is $UW^{-1}V-R=0$, with the analogous right covariance $V$.

There is an explicit terminal target kernel, also measurable in any supplied environment. In a terminal mixed block let $\mu$ be the product law of its raw positions, let $s(r)$ be their sum, and let $G>0$ be the sum of the matching Gaussian-position covariances. Given the target block sum $u$, sample the raw-position vector from
$$\frac{q_G(u-s(r))\,\mu(dr)}{\int q_G(u-s(v))\,\mu(dv)}.$$
The denominator is finite and strictly positive everywhere by [F4]. Fill the Gaussian positions conditional on their remaining sum $u-s(r)$: for their covariance matrices $C_j$ and fresh independent $h_j\sim N(0,C_j)$, put $H_0=\sum_jh_j$ and $g_j=C_jG^{-1}(u-s(r))+h_j-C_jG^{-1}H_0$. The residual vector has sum zero, zero cross covariance with $H_0$, and covariance blocks $\delta_{ij}C_i-C_iG^{-1}C_j$; thus [F4] identifies its Gaussian conditional law. Multiplying the posterior by the total-sum density and integrating in $u$ proves the original raw/Gaussian product law, first on rectangles and then by monotone approximation. This verifies the terminal conditional law at every sum, without choosing regular conditional versions. Independent terminal kernels and the split laws of step 2.1 consequently recover exactly the entire mixed row product law by induction through the disjoint binary blocks. The existing Gaussian row is unchanged, and already has its required product law.

Use step 1.1 and a union bound for every dyadic target sum and every within-terminal prefix in the completed target and Gaussian rows. There are at most $Cq$ such vectors. Except on probability $C_Kq e^{-c_KL}$, each target sum of size $s$ has norm at most $C_K(\sqrt{sL}+BL)$. The target residual is $D_I=VW^{-1}S_L-UW^{-1}S_R$, so its norm satisfies the same bound with a different $C_K$. At active sizes $s\ge2q_0$, choose $H_K$ large enough that these target norms are at most $c_Ks/B$; their ratios to $s/B$ are bounded by $C_K/\sqrt{H_K}+C_K/H_K$. Their squared norms divided by $s$ are at most $C_KL$. Step 1.3 therefore bounds the root discrepancy and every residual discrepancy $\delta_I=D_I-E_I$ by $C_KBL$. The within-terminal prefix norms are at most $C_K(\sqrt{q_0L}+BL)\le C_KBL$, since $q_0<2H_KB^2L$. No conditional concentration inside a terminal block has been assumed.

Write $e_I=S_I-V_I$. Its child equations are $e_L=UW^{-1}e_I+\delta_I$ and $e_R=VW^{-1}e_I-\delta_I$. For a prefix $P$ ending at a terminal boundary of $I$, let $C_P$ be the sum of its individual covariance matrices. Its discrepancy has the exact expansion
$$\sum_{i\in P}(X_i-G_i)=C_PW_I^{-1}e_I+\sum_{J\text{ on the boundary path}}M_{J,P}\delta_J.$$
If the boundary lies in the left child, $M_{J,P}=C_{\rm partial\ left}W_{J_L}^{-1}$; if it lies in the right child, $M_{J,P}=I-C_{\rm partial\ right}W_{J_R}^{-1}$. To prove the formula, in the left case substitute the child's leading term $C_PU^{-1}e_L$ and cancel $U^{-1}U$; in the right case add $e_L$ to $C_QV^{-1}e_R$, obtaining leading coefficient $(U+C_Q)W^{-1}$ and residual coefficient $I-C_QV^{-1}$. Induction from terminal blocks proves the expansion. This cancellation uses the order $W_{\rm desc}W_{\rm parent}^{-1}W_{\rm parent}W_{\rm grandparent}^{-1}$ and never commutes two matrices. If a partial child has $r$ of its $h$ entries, its coefficient norm is at most $Kr/h\le K$. Hence $\|M_{J,P}\|\le1+K$ and $\|C_PW_I^{-1}\|\le K$. There are at most $\log_2q$ boundary ancestors. The expansion and step 3.1 give terminal-boundary error $C_KBL\log(eq)$; adding its terminal prefix residual gives the same bound for all prefixes.

If $q<2q_0$, couple a raw or mixed row independently to a matching Gaussian row. Their unconditional concentration bounds from step 1.1 and a union bound over prefixes give maximum discrepancy at most $C_K(\sqrt{qL}+BL)\le C_KBL$ except on probability $C_Kq e^{-c_KL}$. This covers the small sizes, including a row of one entry, and large $B$. Thus in all cases a mixed row can be coupled directly to an already realized matching Gaussian row with stage error at most $C_KBL\log(eq)$ and bad probability at most $C_Kq e^{-c_KL}$.

Pad the initial length $m$ to dyadic $q<2m$ by independent $N_d(0,I_d)$ entries; for $m=1$ take $q=1$. These added laws have empty atom sums and preserve all covariance bounds. Begin with its matching independent Gaussian row. At an active length at least $2q_0$, apply steps 2.1–3.2, taking the target laws to be the designated raw laws in even slots and matching Gaussians in odd slots. Use the root and residual primitives computed from the already realized active Gaussian row, and fresh target terminal kernels. Freeze the newly raw even positions and retain the odd Gaussian positions in their compressed order. Their covariance matrices still lie between $I$ and $KI$. The target product law and [F7] preserve independence of the active row from its frozen complement. At an active length below $2q_0$, independently replace all remaining Gaussian positions by their designated raw laws, using step 3.3, and stop. This constructs the full intended independent raw row after at most $C\log(eN)$ stages, without changing the original Gaussian row.

Every original prefix meets the active positions of each stage in an initial compressed prefix. Triangle inequality adds the stage maximum errors, each at most $C_KBL\log(eN)$, to give total error at most $C_{A,K}B\log^3(eN)$. Always use the ambient $L=a\log(eN)$, even for short compressed rows. The union bad probability is at most $C_KN\log(eN)e^{-c_Ka\log(eN)}$. Choose $a$ sufficiently large depending only on $A,K$ to make this at most $N^{-A}$ for all $N\ge1$; then restrict to the first $m$ entries. This proves the numerical assertion.

For the parameter assertion, every entry law is a measurable kernel obtained by applying addition to the finite product of its supplied atom and Gaussian kernels, using [F5]. Covariance entries are measurable integrals. In dimensions one and two positive definite inverse square roots are continuous functions of their matrices: in dimension two, for $C>0$, $C^{1/2}=(C+\sqrt{\det C}\,I)/\sqrt{\operatorname{tr}C+2\sqrt{\det C}}$, as verified in an eigenbasis by [F3]; the semidefinite zero case is defined by zero and the formula extends continuously. Thus the Gaussian starts and all transforms in steps 1.2–1.3 depend measurably on the parameter. Mixed transformed joint and prefix densities are Gaussian convolution integrals of their raw product kernels, so are jointly measurable by [F5] and strictly positive. Their conditional CDFs are measurable density-ratio integrals. The coordinate quantiles in [F2] are measurable rational infima of those CDFs; hence its root and residual maps are jointly measurable in the parameter and all spatial inputs. The terminal posterior in step 2.2 is likewise a measurable kernel with positive measurable denominator, followed by the explicit Gaussian bridge kernel. Finite kernel products and successive extensions preserve measurability: for one extension define its law by integrating the next kernel against the preceding law; [F5] gives measurable evaluations and [F6] gives countable additivity by monotone convergence of disjoint indicator sums. Iterating this finite construction gives a coupling kernel $Q_\theta$, and every previous marginal and probability bound holds at each parameter. No pointwise selection of conditional-law versions or coupling laws is used.

boundaries.evidence: An atom sum may be empty and every original Gaussian term may vanish; matching covariance Di>=I still ensures the core root and anchor covariances are positive definite.
Zero atoms and zero original Gaussian terms are allowed. The matrix inverses are only of block covariances W,R and Gaussian anchor aggregates, all explicitly positive definite.
m=N=1 and a one-entry active row are handled by the independent short-row coupling and Bernstein bound, with ambient log(eN)>=1.
Individual atoms and original Gaussian terms may be degenerate. Their total entry covariances lie between I and KI; the mixed Gaussian anchors whiten to a fixed positive covariance fraction.
The integer lengths m<=N, K=1, and weak covariance/atom bounds are included. Constants are chosen before the union bound and uniformly cover all finite N.

AC is explicit and inherited. Matrix square roots, parameterwise quantiles, and terminal posteriors are explicit measurable constructions; no unmeasurable pointwise selection of conditional kernels is used.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Fix $K\ge1$ and $A>0$. There is a finite $C_{A,K}$ such that the following holds uniformly over $1\le d\le2$, integers $1\le m\le N$, and $B\ge1$. Let $X_1,\ldots,X_m$ be independent centered vectors with representations
$$X_i=Z_i+\sum_{r=1}^{r_i}Y_{ir},\qquad |Y_{ir}|\le B\ \hbox{almost surely},$$
where every $r_i$ is finite, all displayed atom and Gaussian terms are independent, every $Y_{ir}$ is centered, and every $Z_i$ is a centered Gaussian vector, possibly degenerate. Suppose
$$I_d\le D_i:=\operatorname{cov}(X_i)\le KI_d.$$
There is a coupling with independent $G_i\sim N_d(0,D_i)$ satisfying
$$\Pr\!\left(\max_{1\le k\le m}\left|\sum_{i=1}^k(X_i-G_i)\right|>C_{A,K}B\log^3(eN)\right)\le N^{-A}.$$
The constants do not depend on the atom counts or individual laws. Empty atom sums and zero Gaussian terms are allowed.

The coupling laws can be chosen as a measurable probability kernel in a supplied standard Borel parameter $\theta$: if the atom laws and Gaussian covariance matrices are measurable kernels and functions of $\theta$, with the hypotheses holding for each $\theta$, there is a coupling kernel $Q_\theta(dx,dg)$ with the stated product marginals and the displayed bound for each $\theta$. Thus a random environment with these conditional independent atom laws can first be sampled, and this coupling kernel then applied conditionally. This assertion concerns the conditional laws supplied in the hypotheses and does not assume a selection of regular conditional laws separately at each parameter.

Assume AC. For every $A>0$ there is a finite constant $C_A$, independent of all row laws and lengths, such that the following holds. Let $1\le d\le2$, $N\ge1$, $B\ge1$, and let $X_1,\ldots,X_N$ be independent random vectors in $\mathbb R^d$ with
$$EX_i=0,\qquad \operatorname{cov}(X_i)=I_d,\qquad |X_i|\le B\quad\hbox{almost surely}.$$
Their distributions need not be identical. There is a coupling with independent $G_1,\ldots,G_N\sim N_d(0,I_d)$ such that
$$\Pr\!\left(\max_{1\le k\le N}\left|\sum_{i=1}^k(X_i-G_i)\right|>C_AB\log^3(eN)\right)\le N^{-A}.$$
The coupling can be realized on an extension preserving an already realized raw row as its original marginal. Independence between the raw and Gaussian rows is not asserted.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be independent centered square-integrable real random variables. Suppose $b\ge0$ is finite and $|X_i|\le b$ almost surely for each $i$. Put $v=\sum_{i=1}^n\operatorname{Var}(X_i)$. For $t>0$, if $v>0$ then
$$\mathbb P\left(\left|\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\right|\ge t\right)\le 2\exp\!\left(-\frac{t^2}{2(v+bt/3)}\right),$$
and if $v=0$ then this probability is $0$.

Assume AC. If $\phi:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is finite convex and both $X$ and $\phi(X)$ are integrable, then $\phi(E[X\mid\mathcal G])\le E[\phi(X)\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely; the left side is measurable and integrable.

If $X,Y\in L^2(\mathbb P)$ are real random variables, then
$$\mathbb E[|XY|]\le\big(\mathbb E[X^2]\big)^{1/2}\big(\mathbb E[Y^2]\big)^{1/2}.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $X,Y$ is zero almost surely, or
there is a constant $c>0$ with
$$|X|^2=c\,|Y|^2\qquad\mathbb P\text{-almost surely}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

Assume AC. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then $$\Phi_X(t):=\mathbb E e^{it\cdot X}=\exp(it\cdot m-t^T\Sigma t/2)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R^d).$$ This transform uniquely determines the law, including singular Sigma.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $m\ge1$ be finite, let $d_j\ge1$, and let
$Z_j$ for $1\le j\le m$ be mutually independent random elements of
$\mathbb R^{d_j}$. Suppose $Z_j\sim N_{d_j}(a_j,\Sigma_j)$, where each
$\Sigma_j$ is symmetric positive semidefinite. Put
$D=\sum_{j=1}^m d_j$, $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m)$,
$a=(a_1,\ldots,a_m)$, and
$\Sigma=\operatorname{diag}(\Sigma_1,\ldots,\Sigma_m)$. Then
$$Z\sim N_D(a,\Sigma).$$
No covariance block needs to be invertible.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(U,V)$ be a jointly multivariate-normal real
vector with finite-dimensional blocks $U\in\mathbb R^p$ and
$V\in\mathbb R^q$, where $p,q\ge1$. If $\operatorname{Cov}(U_i,V_j)=0$ for every
$1\le i\le p$ and $1\le j\le q$, then $U$ and $V$ are independent. The
covariance matrix may be singular.

Let $\varphi(x)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2}$ and
$\overline\Phi(x)=\int_x^\infty\varphi(y)\,dy$ for $x\in\mathbb R$. Then for
every $x>0$
$$\frac{x\,\varphi(x)}{1+x^2}\ \le\ \overline\Phi(x)\ \le\ \frac{\varphi(x)}{x},$$
and consequently, for every $x>1$,
$$\Bigl(\frac1x-\frac1{x^3}\Bigr)\varphi(x)\ \le\ \overline\Phi(x)\ \le\ \frac{\varphi(x)}{x}.$$
Both bounds are sharp as $x\to\infty$ in the sense that the ratio of each side
to $\overline\Phi(x)$ tends to $1$.

A measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$ is **standard Borel** if there are a Polish space $P$ and a bijection $h:E\to P$ such that $A\in\mathcal E$ exactly when $h[A]$ is Borel in $P$. Thus the measurable structure is part of the datum; no particular compatible Polish topology on $E$ is selected.
Every finite product of standard Borel spaces, with its finite product sigma-algebra, is standard Borel.

For every natural $n\ge1$, let $\mathbb R^n$ be the set of functions
$x:n\to\mathbb R$ with its finite-product topology and Borel sigma-algebra
([[def-product-topology]], [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). Then
$(\mathbb R^n,\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n))$ is standard Borel.

Assume AC. Let $\lambda$ be a probability on $(E\times T,\mathcal S\otimes\mathcal T)$, where E and T are standard-Borel spaces, and let $\beta(B)=\lambda(E\times B)$ be its second marginal. There is a probability kernel $K:(T,\mathcal T)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ such that

$$\lambda(A\times B)=\int_B K(y,A)\,\beta(dy)\quad(A\in\mathcal S,\ B\in\mathcal T).$$

It is unique as a kernel outside a single measurable $\beta$-null set. For every nonnegative product-measurable $f:E\times T\to[0,\infty]$,

$$\int f(x,y)\,\lambda(d(x,y))=\int_T\left(\int_E f(x,y)K(y,dx)\right)\beta(dy).$$

In particular this applies to the joint law of random elements $(X,Y)$, with $\beta=P_Y$; the direction is the law of X given Y.

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

Let $(S,\Sigma)$ and $(T_i,\Tau_i)$ for $i<n$ be measurable spaces, with
$n<\infty$, and let $K_i:S\to T_i$ be probability kernels with the same
source. There is a unique probability kernel
$$K:S\to\prod_{i<n}T_i$$
whose evaluation on every measurable rectangle is
$$K(s,\prod_{i<n}B_i)=\prod_{i<n}K_i(s,B_i).$$
For $n=0$, the target is the empty-product singleton and $K$ is its point
mass. For $n>0$, the product sigma-algebra is the recursive finite product
sigma-algebra.

Assume Choice. Let $(E_n,\mathcal E_n)_{n\ge0}$ be measurable spaces, let
$\mu_0$ be a probability measure on $E_0$, and, for each $n\ge0$, let $K_n$ be
a probability kernel from $E_0\times\cdots\times E_n$ to $E_{n+1}$. There is a
unique probability measure $P$ on
$$ \left(\prod_{n\ge0}E_n,\ \bigotimes_{n\ge0}\mathcal E_n\right) $$ whose finite-prefix laws are the prescribed iterated integrals $$ \mu_0(dx_0)K_0(x_0,dx_1)K_1(x_0,x_1,dx_2)\cdots K_{r-1}(x_0,\ldots,x_{r-1},dx_r). $$
In particular, if every $E_n=E$ and
$K_n(x_0,\ldots,x_n,A)=K(x_n,A)$, the coordinate process is a homogeneous
$K$-chain with initial law $\mu_0$.

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

For every finite family of events $A_0,\ldots,A_{n-1}$,
$$\mathbb P\!\left(\bigcup_{i<n}A_i\right)\le\sum_{i<n}\mathbb P(A_i).$$
For $n=0$ both sides are $0$.

Let $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be measurable sets in a measure space. If the nonnegative extended sum satisfies

$$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k)<+\infty,$$

then

$$\mu\left(\limsup_{k\to\infty}E_k\right)=0.$$

No independence hypothesis and no finiteness hypothesis on the whole space are required.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and let $d\ge1$ be finite.

1. A standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion exists: one may take $d$
   independent copies of the constructed one-dimensional Brownian path and
   assemble them coordinatewise.
2. If $B$ is any standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion and $c>0$, then
   $$Y_t=c^{-1/2}B_{ct},\qquad t\ge0,$$
   is again standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion. Moreover, the random
   elements $B$ and $Y$ have the same law on $(\mathbb R^d)^{[0,\infty)}$
   equipped with its cylinder sigma-algebra.

Assume countable choice and dependent choice. For probability spaces
$(E_n,\mathcal E_n,\mu_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ there is a unique probability measure
$\mu$ on $\mathcal C_{\mathbb N}$ such that, for every finite $F$, its
$F$-coordinate marginal is $\bigotimes_{n\in F}\mu_n$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and let $d\ge1$ be a finite integer. An
$\mathbb R^d$-valued process $B=(B_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **standard
$d$-dimensional Brownian motion** if:

1. $B_0=0$ almost surely;
2. for every finite list $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_n$, the vector increments
   $$B_{t_j}-B_{t_{j-1}},\qquad 1\le j\le n,$$
   are mutually independent and have laws
   $N_d(0,(t_j-t_{j-1})I_d)$; and
3. there is one measurable event $A$ with $P(A)=1$ such that
   $t\mapsto B_t(\omega)$ is continuous from $[0,\infty)$ to
   $\mathbb R^d$ for every $\omega\in A$.

Equivalently, its $d$ coordinate processes $B^\alpha=(B_t^\alpha)_{t\ge0}$
are independent standard one-dimensional Brownian motions. Here independence
of the processes means the following precise assertion. Put
$I=[0,\infty)$ and equip $\mathbb R^I$ with its cylinder sigma-algebra. The
maps
$$ \Phi_\alpha:\Omega\longrightarrow\mathbb R^I, \qquad \Phi_\alpha(\omega)(t)=B_t^\alpha(\omega), \qquad 1\le\alpha\le d, $$
are independent random elements.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

derivations.claim:
Write $a(x)=\int h(x,y)
u(dy)$, $b(y)=\int h(x,y)
u(dx)$ and $c(x,y)=h(x,y)-a(x)-b(y)$, defining them arbitrarily on the null sets where the integrals are not finite. By [F4], they are measurable, have finite $q$th moments, are centered, and $\mathbb E[c(U,V)\mid U]=\mathbb E[c(U,V)\mid V]=0$ for independent $U,V$ of law $
u$. Expanding the products using these two zero conditional means gives
$$\Gamma=\operatorname{cov}(a(U)+b(U))+\operatorname{cov}(c(U,V))\ge0.$$
Indeed the variance of $h(U,V)$ is the sum of the covariances of $a(U)$, $b(V)$ and $c(U,V)$, while the lag-one covariance is $\mathbb E[b(U)a(U)^T]$. This proves both the displayed identity and nonnegativity without any limit theorem.

For a deterministic orthonormal basis of $\ker\Gamma$, step 1.1's sum of nonnegative scalar variances implies that each basis component of $c$ is zero almost surely and the same component of $a+b$ is zero almost surely. Hence the kernel projection of $h(U_i,U_{i+1})$ is $a_0(U_i)-a_0(U_{i+1})$, where $a_0$ is the kernel projection of $a$. It is an exact endpoint coboundary simultaneously for all $i$, after removing a countable union of null sets. Its partial sums are $a_0(U_0)-a_0(U_k)$. For every $\epsilon>0$, the union and Markov bounds over $k\le2^j$ give probability at most $C\epsilon^{-q}2^{j(1-q/p)}$ that their maximum exceeds $\epsilon2^{j/p}$. This is summable, so [F7], first for rational $\epsilon>0$ and then for all $n$ between successive powers of two, gives maximum $o(n^{1/p})$. If $\Gamma=0$ take $G_i=0$ and adjoin a Brownian motion by [F8]. Otherwise work in its deterministic positive-covariance range of dimension one or two and later restore this kernel projection.

For independent anchors $A,B$ and interior variables $V,W$, all of law $\nu$, put $Y=h(A,V)-a(A)+h(V,W)+h(W,B)-b(B)$. Its conditional mean given $A,B$ is zero. Its average conditional covariance is
$$\Gamma_*:=\mathbb E\operatorname{cov}(Y\mid A,B)=2\operatorname{cov}(a(U)+b(U))+3\operatorname{cov}(c(U,V)).$$
To check this, substitute the decomposition from step 1.1 to write $Y=(a+b)(V)+(a+b)(W)+c(A,V)+c(V,W)+c(W,B)$. Every cross product vanishes after integrating an endpoint using the zero conditional means of $c$; the five individual covariance contributions give the formula. Thus $2\Gamma\le\Gamma_*\le3\Gamma$, so $\Gamma_*$ is positive definite on the range retained in step 1.2. A fixed invertible linear map there makes $\Gamma_*=I$; its inverse will be restored at the end, and all subsequent constants may depend on this fixed map.

Choose fixed $p<\beta<\alpha<q$, and consider an epoch of $N=2^j$ consecutive triple indices. Put $R=N^{1/\alpha}$, $L=K\log(eN)$ and $m=\lceil R^2L\rceil$. In this epoch replace the normalized active $h$ by $f=h\mathbf1_{\{|h|\le R\}}-\mathbb E[h\mathbf1_{\{|h|\le R\}}]$. Then $|f|\le2R$, $\mathbb E|f|^q\le C$, and its means $a_R,b_R$ and degenerate component $c_R$ have uniformly bounded $q$th moments by [F4]. They converge in $L^2$ to their untruncated versions: the squared tail is at most $R^{2-q}\mathbb E|h|^q$, and conditional averaging is an $L^2$ contraction by coordinatewise [F4]. Consequently the average conditional triple-noise covariance $\Gamma_{*,R}=2\operatorname{cov}(a_R+b_R)+3\operatorname{cov}(c_R)$ tends to $I$. For all sufficiently large deterministic epochs, $c_0I\le\Gamma_{*,R}\le C_0I$ for fixed $c_0,C_0>0$. Finitely many earlier epochs can be coupled arbitrarily and contribute only finite errors.

Let $A_t=U_{3t}$, $V_t=U_{3t+1}$ and $W_t=U_{3t+2}$ in the epoch, relabeling its first triple index as zero. Conditional on its anchors $(A_0,\ldots,A_N)$, the interior pairs $(V_t,W_t)$ are independent, and the centered triple noises
$$Y_t=f(A_t,V_t)-a_R(A_t)+f(V_t,W_t)+f(W_t,A_{t+1})-b_R(A_{t+1})$$
are independent centered vectors bounded by $CR$. Define the symmetric matrices $Q(z)=\operatorname{cov}(f(V,W)+f(W,z)-b_R(z))$ and $P(z)=\operatorname{cov}(f(z,V)-a_R(z))+\operatorname{cov}(f(z,V),f(V,W))+\operatorname{cov}(f(V,W),f(z,V))$, where these covariances integrate independent $V,W$. The left and right endpoint terms are independent given the anchors, so
$$V_t:=\operatorname{cov}(Y_t\mid A_t,A_{t+1})=P(A_t)+Q(A_{t+1}),\qquad D_t:=P(A_t)+Q(A_t)=\operatorname{cov}(Y(A_t,A_t)\mid A_t).$$
Although $P$ need not be positive semidefinite, $V_t,D_t,Q(A_t)$ are positive semidefinite, their norms are at most $CR^2$, and $\mathbb EV_t=\mathbb ED_t=\Gamma_{*,R}$. Moreover, for every interval of triple indices,
$$\sum_{t=u}^{v-1}(V_t-D_t)=Q(A_v)-Q(A_u).$$
These are identities of measurable anchor functions, by [F4] and [F6].

Divide the epoch into consecutive chunks of length $m$, leaving a shorter final chunk. The entries of $V_t$ are one-dependent functions of adjacent iid anchors, while $D_t$ are iid functions of individual anchors. For a positive semidefinite matrix $T$ of norm at most $CR^2$, $|T_{uv}|^2\le T_{uu}T_{vv}\le CR^2T_{uu}$. Its entrywise second moments here are therefore at most $CR^2$, because the mean matrices in step 2.2 are uniformly bounded. Within each parity the entries of $V_t$ are independent. Apply [F3] separately to both parities and each matrix entry, and to the independent entries of $D_t$ across $t$. For any full chunk $I$, the probability that an entry of either centered covariance sum exceeds a fixed small multiple of $m$ is at most $C\exp(-cm/R^2)$. Since $\|T\|_{\rm op}\le d\max_{u,v}|T_{uv}|$ for symmetric matrices in dimension $d\le2$, choose the multiplier small relative to $c_0$ and union over at most $N$ chunks and their entries. Choosing $K$ sufficiently large gives an anchor event of probability at least $1-N^{-A}$, for any prescribed $A>0$, on which
$$c_1mI\le\sum_{t\in I}V_t\le C_1mI,\qquad c_1mI\le\sum_{t\in I}D_t\le C_1mI$$
for every full chunk, with both sums bounded on both sides. The same entrywise Bernstein calculation gives an upper bound $C_1mI$ on both sums in the shorter chunk. Here and below the constants may be enlarged independently of $N$ and $R$. Since $\alpha>2$, $m<N$ eventually; if not, the same upper bound handles the entire epoch as one residual chunk.

On a good anchor vector, divide each full-chunk sum of $Y_t$ by $\sqrt{c_1m}$. Its conditional covariance lies between $I$ and $KI$, for a fixed $K$, and it is a sum of independent centered atoms of norm at most $CR/\sqrt m\le C$. Its whole value need not be bounded. Its atom kernels are the measurable pushforwards of $\nu\otimes\nu$ under the formula in step 2.2; independence holds conditional on the supplied anchors. Thus [F1], with the ambient length parameter $N$ and a fixed atom bound $B\ge\max(1,C)$, supplies a measurable coupling of the chunk sums with independent matching Gaussian chunk sums. Undoing the normalization gives maximum chunk-boundary error at most $C\sqrt m\log^3(eN)\le CR\log^{7/2}(eN)$, with conditional failure at most $N^{-A}$. On bad anchors use independent product coupling instead, preserving both marginals. No theorem about uniformly bounded grouped values is being invoked.

Fill a Gaussian chunk of total covariance $S>0$ and coupled sum $z$ with increments of individual covariances $V_t$ by taking independent $H_t\sim N(0,V_t)$ and setting $H'_t=H_t+V_tS^{-1}(z-\sum H_t)$. The residual $H_t-V_tS^{-1}\sum H_t$ is independent of the original total Gaussian by [F5]; direct covariance calculation shows this is its exact conditional bridge law and its sum is $z$. Thus the completed Gaussian noise row has exactly its conditional independent Gaussian product law. Conditional on good anchors, every within-chunk raw prefix has atom bound $CR$ and covariance at most $C_1mI$. Coordinatewise [F3] and Gaussian tails in [F5], with a union bound over at most $N$ prefixes, bound both raw and Gaussian within-chunk norms by $C(\sqrt{mL}+RL)\le CRL$, with failure at most $N^{-A}$ after enlarging $K$. Couple a shorter residual chunk independently and use its covariance upper bound in the same calculation. Consequently there is a conditional noise-row coupling $Y_t\leftrightarrow Z_t^V$, with $Z_t^V$ conditionally independent $N(0,V_t)$, of full-prefix error $CR\log^{7/2}(eN)$ and total failure $CN^{-A}$. Its extension to the actually given $Y_t$ follows by [F6] disintegrating the finite joint law given anchors and $Y_t$; the original innovations are preserved.

To redistribute covariance without a matrix random clock, start instead with independent standard Gaussian vectors $Z_t$, independent of the anchors, and put $Z_t^D=D_t^{1/2}Z_t$. These have the required conditional independent $D_t$ row law even if individual $D_t$ are singular. On good anchors group them into the same full chunks, whose covariances $B_i=\sum D_t$ are positive definite. Write $A_i=\sum V_t$ for the desired other row. Pad to a dyadic number of chunks with independent identical-covariance $mI$ Gaussian entries in both rows. All chunk covariances lie between $c_1mI$ and $C_1mI$, and every contiguous whole-chunk interval satisfies $\|A_I-B_I\|\le CR^2$ by step 2.2's endpoint identity; padded intervals retain that bound. We construct the $A$ row from the already given $B$ row using the Gaussian tree in the next two steps, leaving the original $Z_t$ unchanged.

At a node of $s$ chunks and for either covariance row $C$, write $C_P=C_L+C_R$, $H_C=C_LC_P^{-1}$, and $T_C=C_L-C_LC_P^{-1}C_L=(C_L^{-1}+C_R^{-1})^{-1}$. Thus $C_P$ and $T_C$ have eigenvalues comparable to $sm$, and the Gaussian parent and residual $S_L-H_CS_P$ are independent by [F5]. Extract their standardized independent Gaussian primitives from the given $B$ row, and use the same primitives to construct the $A$ root and residuals. For positive definite matrices $M,N$, the identity $M^{1/2}X+XN^{1/2}=M-N$, with $X=M^{1/2}-N^{1/2}$, yields $\|X\|\le C\|M-N\|/(\sqrt{\lambda_{\min}M}+\sqrt{\lambda_{\min}N})$: solve it by integrating $e^{-tM^{1/2}}(M-N)e^{-tN^{1/2}}$ and bound the integral. The endpoint bounds in step 3.1 and the inverse identity imply $\|H_A-H_B\|\le CR^2/(sm)$, $\|T_A-T_B\|\le CR^2$, and $\|T_A^{1/2}-T_B^{1/2}\|\le CR^2/\sqrt{sm}$. A union bound over the Gaussian parents and primitives gives, outside probability $N^{-A}$, $|S_P^B|\le C\sqrt{smL}$ and primitive norms at most $C\sqrt L$. Reconstruct children by $S_L^C=H_CS_P^C+T_C^{1/2}z_I$ and $S_R^C=S_P^C-S_L^C$. Their errors satisfy $e_L=H_Ae_P+\eta_I$, $e_R=(I-H_A)e_P-\eta_I$, with $|\eta_I|\le CR^2\sqrt{L/(sm)}\le CR$, and the root error is also at most $CR$. Every child and root marginal is its exact Gaussian law, so the two completed chunk rows each have their required conditional product law.

The prefix bound uses exact covariance interpolation, not repeated norm bounds on $H_A$. In any subtree its leading root coefficient is $A_{\mathrm{prefix}}A_P^{-1}$. At a boundary ancestor its residual coefficient is $A_{\mathrm{partial\ left}}A_L^{-1}$ if the boundary is in the left child, and $I-A_{\mathrm{partial\ right}}A_R^{-1}$ if it is in the right child. For the left case substitute the child's leading term and cancel $A_L^{-1}A_L$; for the right case add the full left error to the partial right error, giving leading coefficient $(A_L+A_{\mathrm{partial\ right}})A_P^{-1}$ and the stated residual coefficient. This proves the expansion by induction. Each coefficient has norm at most $1+C_1/c_1$, using the count and eigenvalue bounds on chunk covariances, and there are at most $C\log(eN)$ boundary ancestors. Step 3.2 therefore gives prefix error $CR\log(eN)$ at chunk boundaries. Fill the $V_t$ Gaussian increments by the bridge in step 2.5; the $D_t$ increments were already present. Their within-chunk prefix norms are at most $C\sqrt{mL}\le CRL$ by Gaussian tails and the covariance upper bounds. Handle a short residual chunk independently. This gives full-prefix Gaussian-row error $CR\log(eN)$ outside probability $CN^{-A}$. On bad anchors use an independent $V_t$ row while retaining the original independent standard $Z_t$. All operations are measurable matrix functions and finite Gaussian kernels.

The couplings of steps 2.5 and 3.3 have the same joint anchor and $V_t$-Gaussian-row marginal. Disintegrate the second joint law to give its standard $Z$ row conditional on that common anchor and Gaussian row, and append it to the first coupling. The disintegration formula in [F6] proves that both joint laws, hence both error estimates, are preserved. In particular the original innovations remain unchanged and the $Z_t$ row is still independent standard Gaussian conditional on anchors. The two full-prefix errors add. Adding back the conditional means of the triples now gives an iid replacement row
$$L_t=D_t^{1/2}Z_t+a_R(A_t)+b_R(A_t),$$
since the pairs $(A_t,Z_t)$ are iid. Indeed the original mean sum is $\sum_{t<k}(a_R(A_t)+b_R(A_{t+1}))=\sum_{t<k}(a_R(A_t)+b_R(A_t))+b_R(A_k)-b_R(A_0)$. The endpoint means have uniformly bounded $q$th moments by step 2.1. Their maximum exceeds $R$ with probability at most $CN R^{-q}$ by [F7]. Therefore the original truncated triple sums and the partial sums of $L_t$ have maximum error $CR\log^{7/2}(eN)$ with failure at most $CN^{-A}+CN R^{-q}$.

The row $L_t$ is centered and has uniformly bounded $q$th moment: conditional Gaussian moments and coordinatewise [F4] give $\mathbb E\|D_t\|^{q/2}\le C\mathbb E|Y(A_t,A_t)|^q\le C\mathbb E|f(U,V)|^q\le C$, and the mean terms satisfy the same bound. Write $\gamma_0=\mathbb E[f(U_0,U_1)f(U_0,U_1)^T]$, $\gamma_1=\mathbb E[f(U_0,U_1)f(U_1,U_2)^T]$, and $\Gamma_R=\gamma_0+\gamma_1+\gamma_1^T$. The variance of a triple is $3\gamma_0+2(\gamma_1+\gamma_1^T)$. Subtracting the covariance of its conditional mean $a_R(A_0)+b_R(A_1)$ gives $\mathbb ED_t$ by total variance. Since $\mathbb E[b_R(U)a_R(U)^T]=\gamma_1$, adding $\operatorname{cov}(a_R+b_R)$ gives
$$\operatorname{cov}(L_t)=3\Gamma_R.$$
This is a direct finite product calculation, independent of convergence in law or an inference from a coupling error. As $R\to\infty$, $\Gamma_R\to\Gamma$, which is positive definite in the active space; hence these iid covariances have fixed upper and positive lower eigenvalue bounds in every sufficiently large epoch.

We derive the finite-horizon iid bound needed for this changing row directly from [F2]. Suppose $T_1,\ldots,T_N$ are iid centered vectors with $\mathbb E|T_1|^q\le M$, and covariance $\Sigma$ whose eigenvalues lie in a fixed $[\lambda,\Lambda]$ with $\lambda>0$. Put $R_2=N^{1/\beta}$ and $T'_i=T_i\mathbf1_{\{|T_i|\le R_2\}}-\mu$, $\mu=\mathbb E[T_1\mathbf1_{\{|T_1|\le R_2\}}]$. The tail union probability is at most $MN R_2^{-q}$, and on its complement the maximum sum correction is at most $MN R_2^{1-q}=O(R_2)$. Also $\Sigma-\Sigma'=\mathbb E[T_1T_1^T\mathbf1_{\{|T_1|>R_2\}}]+\mu\mu^T$, so $\|\Sigma-\Sigma'\|\le C_MR_2^{2-q}$. Uniformly for all sufficiently large $N$ the eigenvalues of $\Sigma'$ are in $[\lambda/2,C]$. The whitened $T'_i$ have covariance $I$ and norm at most $CR_2$, so [F2] yields independent standard $H_i$ with maximum coupling error to $\Sigma'^{1/2}H_i$ at most $C R_2\log^3(eN)$, outside probability $N^{-A}$. All constants are uniform in the iid law under these moment and eigenvalue bounds.

Step 3.2's square-root bound gives $\|\Sigma^{1/2}-\Sigma'^{1/2}\|\le C_MR_2^{2-q}$. Use the same $H_i$ and apply Gaussian tails to all its partial sums to bound the covariance correction by $C_M\sqrt N R_2^{2-q}\sqrt{\log(eN)}$ with failure at most $N^{-A}$. This is $o(R_2)$ because $\beta<q<2(q-1)$. Consequently steps 4.1 and 4.2 give a finite-row iid coupling with matching covariance $\Sigma$, error $C R_2\log^3(eN)$ and failure $CN^{-A}+MN R_2^{-q}$. Apply this result to the varying laws $T_i=L_i$ from step 3.5, using their uniform moment and eigenvalue bounds. This uses no fixed-law asymptotic iid theorem and asserts no triangular-law interface absent from a supplier's Statement.

The original normalized active $h$ and $f$ agree up to their global mean correction unless one of the epoch's $3N$ observations exceeds $R$, an event of probability at most $CN R^{-q}$. The mean correction is at most $CN R^{1-q}=O(R)$. Moreover $\|\Gamma_R-\Gamma\|\le CR^{2-q}$. For the lag-one product difference, use $|h_0h_1^T-f_0f_1^T|\le C(|h_0|+|h_1|)^2\mathbf1_{\{|h_0|+|h_1|>R\}}$ before centering and then include the mean correction. Pointwise the displayed squared tail is at most a constant times the sum of the squared tails of $|h_0|$ and $|h_1|$ above $R/2$, so its expectation is at most $CR^{2-q}\mathbb E|h|^q$. The variance term has the same bound. Since $\Gamma$ is positive definite in the active space, couple the iid Gaussian triple increments of covariance $3\Gamma_R$ from step 4.2 to increments of covariance $3\Gamma$ using the same standard normals. Step 3.2's square-root bound and Gaussian tails make the maximum correction at most $C\sqrt N R^{2-q}\sqrt{\log(eN)}=o(R)$ with failure $N^{-A}$, because $\alpha<q<2(q-1)$. Thus each sufficiently large epoch of original triple sums can be coupled to independent Gaussian increments of covariance $3\Gamma$, with error $C N^{1/\beta}\log^{7/2}(eN)$ and failure at most
$$C N^{-A}+C N^{1-q/\alpha}+C N^{1-q/\beta}.$$
Here $R=N^{1/\alpha}\le N^{1/\beta}$, and all constants are uniform over epochs.

Retain triple index $t=0$ as a finite initial prefix, coupled arbitrarily, and perform the finite constructions on epochs $\{2^j,\ldots,2^{j+1}-1\}$ of triple indices, $j\ge0$, using fresh kernels. Each conditional noise coupling and each Gaussian redistribution has the full conditional product marginal given all anchors. Because the original interior pairs are independent conditional on anchors, their finite-epoch kernel products give a product standard $Z$ law conditional on all anchors. Hence the pairs $(A_t,Z_t)$, and therefore the replacement variables $L_t$ with the deterministic epoch-dependent function in step 3.4, are independent across epochs as well as within them. Each later iid-row coupling is glued through its finite replacement row by [F6]; because these rows are independent, products of their kernels give independent final Gaussian rows across epochs. These statements follow by integrating finite rectangles under the conditional product laws, so no independence is being inferred from an error bound. All anchor sets and row coordinates involved in an epoch are finite standard-Borel products, making these disintegrations legitimate. Apply [F6]'s countable kernel extension with the entire original probability space as its initial coordinate to preserve all original innovations. The failure bounds in step 5.1 are summable over $N=2^j$, since $\beta<\alpha<q$. By [F7], all sufficiently large epochs satisfy their error bounds almost surely; finitely many earlier errors can be included in a finite random constant.

Sum the completed epoch errors and the current partial one. The geometric bound $\sum_{j\le J}2^{j/\beta}(j+1)^{7/2}\le C_\beta2^{J/\beta}(J+1)^{7/2}$ gives a global triple-prefix error $O(n^{1/\beta}\log^{7/2}(en))=o(n^{1/p})$. Map back from the fixed normalization in step 1.3 and restore the covariance-kernel coboundary from step 1.2. Split each independent Gaussian triple increment $H_t\sim N(0,3\Gamma)$ into three increments of covariance $\Gamma$: for each $t$ take a fresh triple $K_{t,0},K_{t,1},K_{t,2}\sim N(0,\Gamma)$, independent across all $t,r$ and of all triple increments, and put $G_{3t+r}=H_t/3+K_{t,r}-(K_{t,0}+K_{t,1}+K_{t,2})/3$. By [F5] these three increments are jointly Gaussian, each has covariance $\Gamma$ and distinct ones have zero cross covariance, so the entire resulting row is independent with covariance $\Gamma$. At nontriple endpoints the original sum changes by at most two $X_i$, and the Gaussian sum by at most two $G_i$. Union and Markov bounds on dyadic ranges, using respectively their finite $q$th moments and arbitrary Gaussian moments, show both maxima are $o(n^{1/p})$, as in step 1.2. This proves the stated full-prefix approximation.

In a fixed orthonormal eigenbasis of $\Gamma$, divide each positive-variance Gaussian coordinate by its fixed standard deviation and add independent standard Gaussian coordinates in the zero-variance directions. This yields independent standard normal vector increments realizing $G_i$ by $\Gamma^{1/2}$. For each integer interval adjoin independent Brownian copies by [F8] and use their bridges $W(t)-tW(1)$, independently of the existing increments. Interpolate the standard Gaussian random walk linearly on that interval plus its bridge. The paths are continuous and direct covariance calculation gives $\min(s,t)I_d$; finite Gaussianity and zero cross covariances give independent normal increments by [F5]. Thus [F8] identifies a standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion, and the fixed eigenbasis map gives $\sum_{i<k}G_i=\Gamma^{1/2}B(k)$ at every integer $k$. This construction also applies when $\Gamma=0$ by adjoining an independent Brownian motion. It does not alter the original-process marginal or any error already proved.

boundaries.reason: The Statement assumes an iid process on a probability space, 1<=d<=2 and positive sample sizes; no empty-dimensional or empty-time asymptotic claim is made.

boundaries.evidence: Steps 1.1–1.2 treat Gamma=0 as an exact endpoint coboundary, with zero Gaussian increments and an independently adjoined Brownian motion. Zero atoms and individual zero D_t matrices cause no inversions.

Finitely many small epochs are coupled arbitrarily and absorbed into a finite almost-sure constant. One-dimensional active covariance ranges are retained, and residual chunks require no lower covariance bound.

Step 1.2 removes only covariance-kernel coboundaries. Steps 3.1–3.4 begin with D_t^(1/2)Z_t even for singular individual D_t, extracting Gaussian primitives only from coarse positive-definite chunk covariances. Step 5.4 fills Brownian covariance-kernel directions independently.
The hypothesis is strict q>p>2; internal p<beta<alpha<q are chosen in step 2.1. Steps 5.3–5.4 cover nontriple endpoints and all integer Brownian times. No assertion at q=p or p=2 is made.

AC is explicit in Statement and A1. Finite standard-Borel disintegrations and countable kernel extensions preserve the entire original innovation process; Gaussian square roots use deterministic finite-dimensional covariance restrictions.

boundaries.reason: The Statement is not a biconditional.
The Statement is not a biconditional.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Let $P$ be a probability kernel on an arbitrary measurable space $(X,\mathcal F)$, with invariant probability $\pi$, finite measurable $M:X\to[0,\infty)$ and $0<r<1$ satisfying
$$\|P^n(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le M(x)r^n\quad(x\in X,\ n\ge1).$$
Let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be finite measurable. For each specified initial law $\mu$, there are a nonempty standard-Borel space $S$, a probability kernel $T$ on $S$, an invariant probability $\widehat\pi$, an initial probability $\widehat\mu$, and finite measurable functions $\varphi:S\to\mathbb R$ and $\widehat M:S\to[0,\infty)$ such that
$$\|T^n(z,\cdot)-\widehat\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le\widehat M(z)r^n\quad(z\in S,\ n\ge1).$$
The complete observation path $(f(X_n))_{n\ge0}$ of a $\mu$-started $P$-chain has the same law as $(\varphi(Y_n))_{n\ge0}$ of a $\widehat\mu$-started $T$-chain. The corresponding stationary observation paths also have the same law, and $\widehat\pi(|\varphi|^a)=\pi(|f|^a)$ for every $a>0$, with infinity allowed. The factor may depend on $\mu$.

Moreover, any joint law of that observation path with a random element of a standard-Borel space can be lifted to an extension preserving the entire original chain probability space and process.

Assume AC. Let $P$ be a probability kernel on a nonempty standard-Borel space $(S,\mathcal S)$, with invariant probability $\pi$, finite measurable $M:S\to[0,\infty)$ and $0<r<1$ such that
$$\|P^n(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le M(x)r^n\quad(x\in S,\ n\ge1).$$
Let $f:S\to\mathbb R$ be finite measurable, with $\pi(f)=0$ and $\pi(|f|^v)<\infty$ for some $v>1$. For every initial law, on an extension preserving the given chain there are an integer $m\ge1$, an almost surely finite delay $D\in m\mathbb N$, a standard-Borel seed space $E$, iid seeds $(U_j)_{j\ge0}$, and measurable finite-word and length functions $W:E^2\to\bigsqcup_{k\ge1}S^k$ and $L:E\to m\mathbb N$ with the following properties.

Put $T_0=D$ and $T_{j+1}=T_j+L(U_j)$. Almost surely, simultaneously for all $j\ge0$,
$$\bigl(X_{T_j},\ldots,X_{T_{j+1}-1}\bigr)=W(U_j,U_{j+1}).$$
Write $L_j=L(U_j)$, $Z_j=\sum_{t=T_j}^{T_{j+1}-1}f(X_t)$, and $H_j=\sum_{t=T_j}^{T_{j+1}-1}|f(X_t)|$. Then $Z_j=z(U_j,U_{j+1})$ and $H_j=h(U_j,U_{j+1})$ for measurable functions $z,h$, and
$$\mathbb E e^{aL_0}<\infty\text{ for some }a>0,\qquad 0<\mu_L:=\mathbb EL_0<\infty,$$
$$\mathbb EZ_0=0,\qquad \mathbb EH_0^q<\infty\quad(1\le q<v).$$
For every nonnegative measurable $b:S\to[0,\infty]$ the full-tour occupation identity is
$$\mathbb E\sum_{t=T_0}^{T_1-1}b(X_t)=\mu_L\pi(b).$$
For each specified initial law, the same $m$, iid seed law, $W,L$ and post-delay tour law can be used also for the invariant initial law $\pi$; only the finite initial segment and coupling change.

In particular $(L_j-\mu_L,Z_j)$ is an adjacent-iid centered vector sequence, while the lengths themselves are iid. Full tour words or rewards are not asserted to be iid. No moment of $D$ or of the initial finite prefix is required, and the construction uses a useful multistep split chosen from $P$ rather than requiring any supplied one-step minorization to have positive stationary mass.

Assume AC. Let $1\le d\le2$, let $(E,\mathcal E)$ be standard Borel, and let $(U_i)_{i\ge0}$ be iid $E$-valued random elements with law $\nu$. Let $h:E^2\to\mathbb R^d$ be measurable with
$$\mathbb E h(U_0,U_1)=0,\qquad \mathbb E|h(U_0,U_1)|^q<\infty$$
for some finite $q>2$. Put $X_i=h(U_i,U_{i+1})$, and define
$$\Gamma=\mathbb E[X_0X_0^T]+\mathbb E[X_0X_1^T]+\mathbb E[X_1X_0^T].$$
Then $\Gamma$ is positive semidefinite. For every fixed $2<p<q$, on an extension preserving the entire original process there are independent centered Gaussian vectors $G_i$ with covariance $\Gamma$ such that
$$\max_{1\le k\le n}\left|\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}(X_i-G_i)\right|=o(n^{1/p})\qquad\hbox{almost surely}.$$
The extension can also carry a standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion $B$ with $\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}G_i=\Gamma^{1/2}B(k)$ for every integer $k\ge0$. Singular $\Gamma$, including $\Gamma=0$, is allowed. Neither the Gaussian row nor $B$ is required to be independent of the original process.

Assume AC. Let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be iid centered vectors in $\mathbb R^2$ with $E\|X_1\|^q<\infty$ for some $q>2$. For any fixed real numbers $2<p<a<q$, on an extension preserving the original process there are independent Gaussian vectors $G_i\sim N_2(0,\Sigma)$, where $\Sigma=EX_1X_1^T$, such that almost surely
$$\max_{1\le k\le n}\left\|\sum_{i=1}^k(X_i-G_i)\right\|=O\bigl(n^{1/a}[\log(en)]^3\bigr)=o(n^{1/p}).$$
The extension can also carry a standard two-dimensional Brownian motion $B$ with $\sum_{i=1}^kG_i=\Sigma^{1/2}B(k)$ for every integer $k\ge0$. Thus, in particular, the partial-sum Brownian approximation error is $O(n^{1/p}\log n)$ almost surely. Singular covariance, including $\Sigma=0$, is permitted. Neither $B$ nor $(G_i)$ is required to be independent of $(X_i)$.

Assume AC. Let $\mathcal G$ be a sigma-algebra on a probability space, let $\lambda>0$, and let $N=(N(t))_{t\ge0}$ be $\mathcal G$-measurable at each time. Suppose $N(0)=0$, its paths are nondecreasing right-continuous integer-valued functions finite on bounded intervals, its increments on disjoint time intervals are independent, and $N(t)-N(s)$ has law $\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda(t-s))$ for $0\le s<t$. Let $B$ be a standard Brownian motion independent of $\mathcal G$.

On an extension preserving the original probability space there is a standard Brownian motion $W$, independent of $\mathcal G$, such that
$$\sup_{0\le t\le n}\left|B(t)-\lambda^{-1/2}W(N(t))\right|=O((\log(n+2))^2)\qquad\text{almost surely as }n\to\infty.$$
The almost-sure bound has a finite random constant and a finite random starting index. In particular $W$ is independent of the entire Poisson clock; $W$ and $B$ are not asserted to be independent.

Fix $q>p>2$. Let $(Z_k)_{k\ge1}$ be identically distributed centered real random variables with $\mathbb E|Z_1|^q<\infty$. Assume either that they are independent, or that they are **one-dependent**, meaning that $\sigma(Z_1,\ldots,Z_k)$ and $\sigma(Z_{k+2},Z_{k+3},\ldots)$ are independent for every $k\ge1$. Put $S_0=0$ and $S_j=\sum_{k=1}^jZ_k$.

There is an event of probability one on which, for every $A>0$ and $d\ge0$, with $r_n=\lceil A n^{1/p}(\log n)^d\rceil$ for $n\ge2$,
$$\max_{\substack{0\le i<j\le n\\j-i\le r_n}}|S_j-S_i|=o(n^{1/p}).$$

Let $T>0$, $\theta>0$, and let $S=(0,T]$ carry its subspace topology and
Borel sigma-algebra. This space is Hausdorff as a subspace of $\mathbb R$;
rational intervals give a countable base; and each $x\in S$ has a compact
neighborhood $[x-\delta,x+\delta]\cap S$ for some $0<\delta<x$. Let $\ell$
be Lebesgue measure restricted to $S$. There exists a Poisson point process
on $S$ with intensity measure $\nu_\theta(B)=\theta\ell(B)$. Its total
count is finite almost surely, its event times have no ties almost surely,
and for every integer $m\ge0$ the joint density of the ordered event times
$$0<t_1<\cdots<t_m\le T,\qquad N(S)=m,$$
with respect to $m$-dimensional Lebesgue measure on the ordered simplex is
$$e^{-\theta T}\theta^m.$$
For $m>0$, conditional on $N(S)=m$, the ordered event times have density
$m!/T^m$. For $m=0$ the empty-pattern probability is $e^{-\theta T}$.

For a finite parameter $\lambda\ge0$, the **Poisson count law**
$\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)$ is the probability measure on
$\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ whose masses are
$$\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)\{k\}=e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^k}{k!},\qquad k\in\mathbb N_0,$$
when $\lambda>0$, and is the point mass at $0$ when $\lambda=0$. The
normalization and the moment and generating-function identities used below are
proved in [[lem-poisson-count-law-normalization-and-moments]]. The separate
extended convention for a Poisson point-process count on a Borel set of infinite
intensity is that the count equals $+\infty$ almost surely; it is not a finite
Poisson probability law.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

For all real $x,y$,
$$\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y).$$

The measurable space $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$ with its usual
topology is standard Borel.
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. A countable product of Polish spaces is Polish, and every $G_\delta$ subspace of a Polish space is Polish.

Assume AC. Let $\lambda$ be a probability on $(E\times T,\mathcal S\otimes\mathcal T)$, where E and T are standard-Borel spaces, and let $\beta(B)=\lambda(E\times B)$ be its second marginal. There is a probability kernel $K:(T,\mathcal T)\to(E,\mathcal S)$ such that

$$\lambda(A\times B)=\int_B K(y,A)\,\beta(dy)\quad(A\in\mathcal S,\ B\in\mathcal T).$$

It is unique as a kernel outside a single measurable $\beta$-null set. For every nonnegative product-measurable $f:E\times T\to[0,\infty]$,

$$\int f(x,y)\,\lambda(d(x,y))=\int_T\left(\int_E f(x,y)K(y,dx)\right)\beta(dy).$$

In particular this applies to the joint law of random elements $(X,Y)$, with $\beta=P_Y$; the direction is the law of X given Y.

Assume Choice. Let $(E_n,\mathcal E_n)_{n\ge0}$ be measurable spaces, let
$\mu_0$ be a probability measure on $E_0$, and, for each $n\ge0$, let $K_n$ be
a probability kernel from $E_0\times\cdots\times E_n$ to $E_{n+1}$. There is a
unique probability measure $P$ on
$$ \left(\prod_{n\ge0}E_n,\ \bigotimes_{n\ge0}\mathcal E_n\right) $$ whose finite-prefix laws are the prescribed iterated integrals $$ \mu_0(dx_0)K_0(x_0,dx_1)K_1(x_0,x_1,dx_2)\cdots K_{r-1}(x_0,\ldots,x_{r-1},dx_r). $$
In particular, if every $E_n=E$ and
$K_n(x_0,\ldots,x_n,A)=K(x_n,A)$, the coordinate process is a homogeneous
$K$-chain with initial law $\mu_0$.

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

Let $\mu$ be a measure and let $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be measurable. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k).$$

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ one also has

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k<m}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k<m}\mu(E_k),$$

including $m=0$, where both sides are $0$.

Let $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be events in a probability space. If
$$\sum_{n=0}^\infty \mathbb P(A_n)<+\infty,$$
then
$$\mathbb P(A_n\ \mathrm{i.o.})=0.$$

No independence hypothesis is needed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. A real process
$B=(B_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **standard Brownian motion** if:

1. $B_0=0$ almost surely;
2. for every finite list $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_n$, the increments
   $B_{t_j}-B_{t_{j-1}}$ are mutually independent and have laws
   $N(0,t_j-t_{j-1})$; and
3. there is one measurable event $A$ with $P(A)=1$ such that
   $t\mapsto B_t(\omega)$ is continuous on $[0,\infty)$ for every
   $\omega\in A$.

By
[[lem-brownian-gaussian-covariance-is-equivalent-to-independent-stationary-normal-increments]],
the first two clauses are equivalent to saying that $B$ is a centered Gaussian
process with covariance $\min(s,t)$. Clause 3 is additional: it cannot be
recovered from finite-dimensional distributions alone.

No filtration is part of this definition. In particular, no completed or
right-continuous filtration and no Markov or martingale assertion is silently
imposed. Modifications and indistinguishability retain the distinct meanings in
[[def-law-modification-and-indistinguishability-of-processes]]. The cases
$n=0$, $t_1=0$, and zero-length increments are respectively vacuous or already
covered by $B_0=0$; the increment list itself is strictly increasing.

Choice is declared because the normal-law and Gaussian/increment-equivalence
interfaces construct and identify normal laws under AC. The continuity clause
selects no path and makes no additional use of choice.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(U,V)$ be a jointly multivariate-normal real
vector with finite-dimensional blocks $U\in\mathbb R^p$ and
$V\in\mathbb R^q$, where $p,q\ge1$. If $\operatorname{Cov}(U_i,V_j)=0$ for every
$1\le i\le p$ and $1\le j\le q$, then $U$ and $V$ are independent. The
covariance matrix may be singular.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. The canonical centered Gaussian coordinate process
with covariance $E[X_sX_t]=\min(s,t)$ has a continuous modification $B$, and
$B$ is a standard Brownian motion. In particular, standard Brownian motion
exists.

Assume countable choice and dependent choice. For probability spaces
$(E_n,\mathcal E_n,\mu_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ there is a unique probability measure
$\mu$ on $\mathcal C_{\mathbb N}$ such that, for every finite $F$, its
$F$-coordinate marginal is $\bigotimes_{n\in F}\mu_n$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, let $B$ be a standard Brownian motion
[[def-brownian-motion]]. Use the everywhere-continuous, zero-start
representative fixed in [[thm-brownian-reflection-principle]]: replace the
path by zero outside a measurable probability-one event of continuity and
zero start, retaining the notation $B$. Let $t>0$ and
$M_t:=\sup_{0\le s\le t}B_s$. This is a finite nonnegative random variable:
continuity gives boundedness on $[0,t]$ and identifies its supremum with the
supremum over the countable dense set $(\mathbb Q\cap[0,t])\cup\{t\}$.
With
$\Phi$ the standard normal distribution function,
$\Phi(x)=N(0,1)((-\infty,x])$
[[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]]
[[def-cumulative-distribution-function-of-a-random-variable]], one has for
every $x\ge0$
$$P(M_t\le x)=2\Phi\!\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt t}\right)-1 .$$
Consequently $M_t$ has the same law as $|B_t|$, and on $x>0$ the law of $M_t$
has the density
$$f(x)=\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi t}}\,\exp\!\left(-\frac{x^2}{2t}\right).$$

Let $\varphi(x)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2}$ and
$\overline\Phi(x)=\int_x^\infty\varphi(y)\,dy$ for $x\in\mathbb R$. Then for
every $x>0$
$$\frac{x\,\varphi(x)}{1+x^2}\ \le\ \overline\Phi(x)\ \le\ \frac{\varphi(x)}{x},$$
and consequently, for every $x>1$,
$$\Bigl(\frac1x-\frac1{x^3}\Bigr)\varphi(x)\ \le\ \overline\Phi(x)\ \le\ \frac{\varphi(x)}{x}.$$
Both bounds are sharp as $x\to\infty$ in the sense that the ratio of each side
to $\overline\Phi(x)$ tends to $1$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $P$ be a probability kernel on a measurable space
$(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ with invariant probability $\pi$. Assume it is
$\phi$-irreducible
([[def-phi-irreducible-chain]]), aperiodic
([[def-general-state-aperiodic-markov-chain]]), and Harris recurrent relative
to its nonzero $\sigma$-finite irreducibility measure $\phi$
([[def-harris-recurrent-markov-chain]]). Suppose $P$ is geometrically
ergodic in the sense of
[[def-geometric-and-uniform-ergodicity-for-mcmc-clt]]. Then there exist a
measurable $M:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ with $\pi(M)<\infty$ and $r\in(0,1)$ such
that
$$\|P^n(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le M(x)r^n\quad(x\in\mathsf X,\ n\ge1).$$

In fact, the same conclusion holds assuming only AC, invariance of $\pi$, and the everywhere finite measurable common geometric-rate bound in [[def-geometric-and-uniform-ergodicity-for-mcmc-clt]], on the original arbitrary measurable space. The construction below derives the needed irreducibility on a restricted sigma-field directly from that bound.

Assume AC. Let $(X_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a stationary time-homogeneous Markov chain
with invariant probability $\pi$. Suppose there are a measurable
$M:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ with $\pi(M)<\infty$ and $r\in(0,1)$ such that
$$\|P^n(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le M(x)r^n\quad\text{for every }x\in\mathsf X,\ n\ge1.$$
Then the strong-mixing coefficient of the stationary process satisfies
$$\alpha_X(n)\le\pi(M)r^n\quad(n\ge1).$$

Let $X=(X_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a strictly stationary process on a measurable state
space and let $h$ be a measurable real-valued function. Put $Y_k=h(X_k)$.
Then $Y$ is strictly stationary and, for every $n\ge1$,
$$\alpha_Y(n)\le\alpha_X(n),\qquad \phi_Y(n)\le\phi_X(n),\qquad \rho_Y(n)\le\rho_X(n),$$
where the coefficients are as in
[[def-mixing-coefficients-for-stationary-markov-chain]].

Assume AC. Let $(Y_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a centered strictly stationary real sequence with $\mathbb E[Y_0^2]<\infty$, and define $S_n=\sum_{k=1}^nY_k$. Each of the following is sufficient:

1. There is $B<\infty$ with $|Y_0|\le B$ almost surely and $\sum_{n\ge1}\alpha_Y(n)<\infty$.
2. For some $\delta>0$, $\mathbb E|Y_0|^{2+\delta}<\infty$ and $\sum_{n\ge1}\alpha_Y(n)^{\delta/(2+\delta)}<\infty$.
3. For some $a\in(0,1)$, $\alpha_Y(n)=O(a^n)$ and $\mathbb E[Y_0^2\log^+|Y_0|]<\infty$, where $\log^+u=\max(0,\log u)$ for $u>0$ and $0\log^+0:=0$.

In each case the covariance series
$$\sigma_Y^2:=\mathbb E[Y_0^2]+2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\operatorname{Cov}(Y_0,Y_k)$$
converges absolutely and is nonnegative, and
$$n^{-1/2}S_n\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma_Y^2).$$
This includes the degenerate law $N(0,0)$ when $\sigma_Y^2=0$, as in [[lem-zero-long-run-variance-gives-degenerate-clt]]. The coefficient $\alpha_Y$ and strict stationarity have the meanings in [[def-mixing-coefficients-for-stationary-markov-chain]].

Let $X_n$ and $Y_n$ be Borel-measurable random elements with values in a metric space $S$, on the same probability space for each $n$, and let $X$ be an $S$-valued Borel-measurable random element. Suppose $d(X_n,Y_n)$ is measurable and $P(d(X_n,Y_n)>\varepsilon)\to0$ for every $\varepsilon$>0. If $X_n\Rightarrow X$, then $Y_n\Rightarrow X$.

Assume AC. If $X$ has law $N(m,\sigma^2)$ with $\sigma\ge0$, then $\varphi_X(t)=\exp(imt-\sigma^2t^2/2)$ for every real $t$. Moreover $\mathbb EX=m$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\sigma^2$, including $\sigma=0$.

Let $(X_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a stationary time-homogeneous Markov chain with invariant probability $\pi$, and let $f$ be real Borel with $\pi(f)=0$ and $\pi(f^2)<\infty$. For $k\ge0$, set $\gamma_k:=\operatorname{Cov}_{\pi}(f(X_0),f(X_k))$. When the Markov-chain CLT $n^{-1/2}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}f(X_k)\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma_f^2)$ holds with finite variance parameter and $\sum_{k\ge1}|\gamma_k|<\infty$, the **covariance long-run variance** is
$$\sigma^2_{\mathrm{LR}}(f):=\gamma_0+2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\gamma_k.$$

This definition does not infer a CLT from covariance summability, or infer that a weak-limit variance equals the covariance sum. Whenever $\sigma^2_{\mathrm{LR}}(f)$ is used as the variance parameter in a CLT or MCSE claim, that equality must be established by the theorem being applied. For example, the local Poisson-equation theorem proves the equality under its square-integrable solution hypotheses.

derivations.claim: Put $P_0=2+\delta$, $Q_0=2+\delta+\varepsilon$, and $f=g-\pi g$. The given moment makes $\pi|g|<\infty$, since $|g|\le1+|g|^{Q_0}$, and the finite-sum power inequality gives $\pi|f|^{Q_0}<\infty$. Choose $P_0<p<q<Q_0$ and set $b=1/p<1/P_0<1/2$. To obtain exactly the requested observation indices, apply [F1] to the chain starting at $X_1$, with its actual initial law, and observable $f$. This gives a standard-Borel factor retaining the full path $(f(X_1),f(X_2),\ldots)$, the stationary path and its moments, and an everywhere finite common geometric bound. Work on this factor until the original-space lift at the end. Apply [F2] there, retaining its finite prefix and integer delay $D$. Define $F(t)$ to be the sum of the first $\lfloor t\rfloor$ centered observations of the retained tail beginning at calendar position $D$, with the empty sum zero. This real-time tail process has cycle lengths $L_j$, centered rewards $Z_j$, envelopes $H_j$, and relative boundaries $T_0=0$, $T_k=\sum_{j<k}L_j$. Then $F(T_k)=\sum_{j<k}Z_j$, $\mathbb EH_0^q<\infty$, and $\mu=\mathbb EL_0\in[1,\infty)$.
