The pair $(Z_j,L_j-\mu)$ is a centered adjacent-iid vector in $L^q$; exponential length moments and $|Z_j|\le H_j$ verify its two coordinate moments. No iid assertion about the full tours is used.

Apply [F3] jointly to $(Z_j,L_j-\mu)$. Write its long-run covariance as $\Gamma=\begin{pmatrix}u&c\\c&s^2\end{pmatrix}\ge0$. Since the lengths are iid, $s^2=\operatorname{Var}(L_0)$; the reward and cross entries still include their actual lag-one terms. The Gaussian approximation gives a continuous centered Gaussian vector process $A$ of covariance $\min(t,r)\Gamma$ such that $\max_{k\le n}|F(T_k)-A_1(k)|=o(n^b)$ and $\max_{k\le n}|T_k-\mu k-A_2(k)|=o(n^b)$. For now suppose $s>0$. Put $a=c/s^2$ and $v^2=u-c^2/s^2\ge0$. Then $B_0=A_2/s$ is standard Brownian. If $v>0$, $B=(A_1-aA_2)/v$ is standard Brownian independent of the entire process $B_0$: each finite stack is jointly Gaussian and every cross-covariance is $(c-as^2)\min(t,r)=0$, so [F10] gives independence on finite rational-time cylinders and continuity extends it to all times. If $v=0$, the residual Gaussian process is zero on rational times almost surely and hence identically zero; adjoin an independent unused $B$. Thus, with independent $B,B_0$, we have $\max_{k\le n}|F(T_k)-a(T_k-\mu k)-vB(k)|=o(n^b)$ and $\max_{k\le n}|T_k-\mu k-sB_0(k)|=o(n^b)$. This regression uses the full $c=\Gamma_{12}$, not just the covariance inside a single cycle.

Define $\gamma=s^2/\mu$ and $\lambda=\mu^2/s^2$, so $\lambda\gamma=\mu$ and $\gamma\sqrt\lambda=s$. Choose any fixed $r>p$ and $r<a_1<q_1<\infty$. Apply [F4] to the centered iid scalar Poisson variables $C_i-\lambda$, embedded as $(C_i-\lambda,0)$, obtaining a joint law with a standard Brownian driver $B'_0$ and $\max_{k\le n}|\sum_{i=1}^kC_i-\lambda k-\sqrt\lambda B'_0(k)|=o(n^{1/r})$. Their moments of every order follow directly from the Poisson exponential series in [F7]. By [F8], disintegrate this joint law to a kernel for the entire count sequence given the integer driver sequence, and evaluate it at the already present $(B_0(k))_{k\ge0}$. This preserves all original variables and reproduces the asserted count/driver joint law. The kernel depends only on $B_0$ and is sampled using new randomness independent of everything earlier, so $B$ remains independent of the joint pair $(B_0,(C_i)_i)$. Conditional on $C_i=m$, insert $m$ independent uniform positions in $(i-1,i]$, independently over unit intervals and of earlier variables given the counts. By [F7] these are the exact finite-window Poisson laws. More explicitly, partitioning a unit interval into lengths $d_j$ gives multinomial conditional counts; summing their mass against $\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)$ yields the product $\prod_j e^{-\lambda d_j}(\lambda d_j)^{k_j}/k_j!$. Hence the resulting locally finite simple right-continuous clock $N$ has independent Poisson increments of rate $\lambda$, $N(k)=\sum_{i\le k}C_i$, and remains independent of $B$ jointly with $B_0$.

We record the uniform estimates used for this clock and for Brownian motion. Summing the Poisson mass series gives $\mathbb E e^{\theta(N(v)-N(u)-\lambda(v-u))}=\exp(\lambda(v-u)(e^\theta-1-\theta))$. The exponential series and $k!\ge2\cdot3^{k-2}$ for $k\ge2$ give $e^\theta-1-\theta\le\theta^2/[2(1-|\theta|/3)]$ for $|\theta|<3$. Exponential Markov with parameter $x/(\lambda(v-u)+x/3)$ and either sign therefore bounds the increment deviation tail by $2\exp[-c_\lambda\min\{x^2/(v-u),x\}]$. On dyadic horizons $n$, take $x=K(\sqrt{(v-u)\log(n+2)}+\log(n+2))$ and union over the at most $(Cn+1)^2$ integer intervals in $[0,Cn]$. A sufficiently large deterministic $K$ makes the probabilities summable, so [F9] proves this bound for all such intervals eventually almost surely, for every positive integer $C$ by countable intersection. In particular unit counts are $O(\log n)$ uniformly, intervals of integer length at least $n^b$ have count increase at least $\lambda/2$ times their length eventually, and $N(t)/t\to\lambda$. Also [F10], a union bound and [F9] make all within-unit Brownian oscillations up to time $Cn$ be $O(\sqrt{\log n})$. These estimates require no independence between evaluation times and the Brownian motion. Consequently the integer coupling in step 2.1 extends to $\sup_{z\le n}|\gamma N(z)-\mu z-sB_0(z)|=o(n^b)$, and step 1.2 gives $\max_{k\le n}|T_k-\gamma N(k)|=o(n^b)$.

Let $m(t)=\max\{k:T_k\le t\}$ and $y(t)=\inf\{z:N(z)>t/\gamma\}$. Brownian reflection on dyadic horizons gives $\sup_{z\le n}|B_0(z)|=O(\sqrt{n\log n})=o(n)$; thus step 1.2 implies $T_k/k\to\mu$. Together with $N(z)/z\to\lambda$, this gives $m(t),y(t)=O(t)$, absorbing their finite initial values. Put $k=\lfloor y(t)\rfloor$. Monotonicity gives $\gamma N(k)\le t<\gamma N(k+1)$, except for an integer endpoint convention which is covered by shifting at most two indices. The unit-count bound in step 2.2 therefore gives $|\gamma N(k)-t|=O(\log n)$ uniformly for $t\le n$. On every required range of $O(n)$ indices, $|T_j-\gamma N(j)|\le n^b$ eventually by its little-o bound. Choose an integer $J$ with $\gamma\lambda J/2>4$. The lower-increment bound in step 2.2 makes a change of $\lceil Jn^b\rceil$ indices change $\gamma N$ by more than $2n^b+O(\log n)$ eventually. The corresponding $T$ values bracket $t$, using index zero at the lower boundary. Thus $\sup_{t\le n}|m(t)-y(t)|=O(n^b)$. The countable estimates for all deterministic horizon multipliers cover a finite random multiplier as well. This is a direct monotone inverse comparison, not an imported renewal approximation.

Let $E_i$ be the interarrival times of $N$. Their iid exponential law follows from [F7]: for $0<t_1<\cdots<t_k\le T$, sum its ordered density over all total counts $m\ge k$ and integrate the last $m-k$ ordered points above $t_k$. The simplex volume is $(T-t_k)^{m-k}/(m-k)!$, so the first-$k$ density is $e^{-\lambda T}\lambda^k\sum_{j\ge0}(\lambda(T-t_k))^j/j!=\lambda^ke^{-\lambda t_k}$. Increasing $T$ covers the whole ordered simplex. The spacing change of variables has determinant one and gives $\prod_{i=1}^k\lambda e^{-\lambda e_i}$ on positive spacings. Hence $\mathbb EE_i=1/\lambda$, $\operatorname{Var}(E_i)=1/\lambda^2$ and all moments are finite, by elementary exponential integration and integration by parts for integer moments, bounding other positive powers by the next integer power plus one. Apply [F4] to $(E_i-1/\lambda,0)$ with the same auxiliary exponent $r>p$, and glue its Brownian driver $V$ to the entire already realized arrival sequence by [F8], using a fresh kernel depending only on that sequence. Then $\max_{k\le n}|\sum_{i=1}^kE_i-k/\lambda-V(k)/\lambda|=o(n^{1/r})$. Since $y(t)=\sum_{i\le\lfloor t/\gamma\rfloor+1}E_i$, set $V_1(t)=\sqrt\gamma V(t/\gamma)$ and use step 2.2's within-unit Brownian bound to obtain $\sup_{t\le n}|y(t)-t/\mu-V_1(t)/(\lambda\sqrt\gamma)|=o(n^b)$. The clock sigma-algebra generated by $B_0,N,V_1$ and their fresh clock randomness remains independent of $B$: each new kernel depended on $B_0$ or on the clock alone and used randomness independent of earlier variables.

Apply [F5] to $B$, $N$ and this entire clock sigma-algebra. It supplies a standard Brownian motion $W^*$ independent of that sigma-algebra, hence independent of $V_1$, and $\sup_{z\le n}|B(z)-\lambda^{-1/2}W^*(N(z))|=O(\log^2(n+2))$. Define $G(t)=(v/\sqrt\lambda)W^*(t/\gamma)-(a\mu/(\lambda\sqrt\gamma))V_1(t)$. It is continuous centered Gaussian with independent stationary increments and variance per unit time $v^2/(\lambda\gamma)+a^2\mu^2/(\lambda^2\gamma)=(v^2+a^2s^2)/\mu=u/\mu$. Thus, when $u>0$, $G=\kappa W$ for a standard Brownian $W$ and $\kappa=\sqrt{u/\mu}$. When $u=0$, positive semidefiniteness forces $a=v=0$, so $G=0$ and adjoin an unused standard $W$. The case $v=0$ needs no residual normalization or nonzero Brownian coefficient.

Two uniform bounds control the remaining calendar errors. By the common $q$th envelope moment and [F9], $\mathbb P(\max_{j\le C2^h}H_j>\eta2^{h/p})\le C'\eta^{-q}2^{h(1-q/p)}$, summable in $h$. Intersecting Borel–Cantelli events over positive rational $\eta$ and integer $C$ yields $\max_{j\le Cn}H_j=o(n^b)$ without any independence requirement. For any standard Brownian motion and fixed $A,C>0$, cover $[0,C2^h]$ by overlapping intervals of length $2A2^{hb}$. Every pair of times at distance at most $A2^{hb}$ lies in one such interval, and [F10] bounds the oscillation tail at $K\sqrt{2^{hb}h}$ by $4e^{-cK^2h}$. There are at most $C'2^{h(1-b)}+2$ intervals. Taking $K$ large and using [F9] gives the uniform modulus $O(n^{b/2}\sqrt{\log n})=o(n^b)$ for windows of length $An^b$; for fixed window length the same proof gives $O(\sqrt{\log n})$. All fixed integer $A,C$ can be placed on one event. Finally [F6] applies to the centered one-dependent rewards $Z_j$, so their partial-sum increments over at most $An^b$ consecutive cycle indices, among the first $Cn$ indices, are uniformly $o(n^b)$. A finite random bound for $A$ or $C$ is covered by their countably many integer choices.

For $y=y(t)$, the following exact decomposition has eight terms: $F(t)-G(t)=\sum_{i=1}^8\Phi_i(t)$, where $\Phi_1=F(t)-F(T_{m(t)})$, $\Phi_2=F(T_{m(t)})-F(T_{\lfloor y\rfloor})$, $\Phi_3=F(T_{\lfloor y\rfloor})-aT_{\lfloor y\rfloor}+a\mu y-vB(y)$, $\Phi_4=a(T_{\lfloor y\rfloor}-\gamma N(y))$, $\Phi_5=-a\mu(y-t/\mu-V_1(t)/(\lambda\sqrt\gamma))$, $\Phi_6=v(B(y)-\lambda^{-1/2}W^*(N(y)))$, $\Phi_7=(v/\sqrt\lambda)(W^*(N(y))-W^*(t/\gamma))$, and $\Phi_8=a(\gamma N(y)-t)$. Adding these expressions cancels every intermediate reward, clock and Gaussian evaluation and leaves exactly $F(t)-G(t)$. This verifies the signs and deterministic drift, including the bounded last term.

Uniformly for $t\le n$, the first term is $o(n^b)$ by the incomplete-cycle bound in [F2] and step 4.1. The second is $o(n^b)$ by the inverse comparison in step 3.1 and [F6]. The third is $o(n^b)$ by step 1.2 at $\lfloor y\rfloor$, the bounded fractional-part drift $a\mu(y-\lfloor y\rfloor)$, and the within-unit Brownian bound. The fourth is $o(n^b)$ by the length/Poisson comparison at $\lfloor y\rfloor$ and the $O(\log n)$ count increase between that point and $y$. The fifth is $o(n^b)$ by step 3.2, and the sixth is $O(\log^2 n)=o(n^b)$ by step 3.3. The strict inverse of the simple Poisson clock satisfies $N(y(t))=\lfloor t/\gamma\rfloor+1$, so its distance from $t/\gamma$ is at most one; step 4.1's fixed-window Brownian bound makes the seventh term $O(\sqrt{\log n})=o(n^b)$, while $|\Phi_8|\le|a|\gamma$. The indices $m(t),y(t)$ are $O(n)$ by step 3.1, so every approximation was evaluated inside its verified range. Therefore $\sup_{t\le n}|F(t)-\kappa W(t)|=o(n^b)$ for $s>0$.

If $s^2=0$, the iid lengths have variance zero, hence $L_j=\mu$ for every $j$ simultaneously almost surely. In particular $T_k=\mu k$; positive semidefiniteness of $\Gamma$ implies $c=0$. The joint approximation [F3] gives $F(T_k)=\sqrt u\,B(k)+o(n^b)$ uniformly for $k\le n$, with a standard Brownian $B$ when $u>0$, and an unused one when $u=0$. For $t\le n$, $m(t)=\lfloor t/\mu\rfloor$, so step 4.1's fixed-window modulus replaces $B(m(t))$ by $B(t/\mu)$ at error $o(n^b)$. The incomplete-tour bound is again $o(n^b)$. Thus $\sup_{t\le n}|F(t)-\sqrt u B(t/\mu)|=o(n^b)$. The process $W(t)=\sqrt\mu B(t/\mu)$ is standard Brownian by its continuous Gaussian covariance and increments, and the coefficient is the same $\kappa=\sqrt{u/\mu}$. This proves the tail approximation in every covariance case, including a zero residual or zero full Gaussian covariance, without inverting a singular matrix.

Restore the finite initial segment of [F2]. Let $A$ be its finite centered reward and $D$ its finite integer length. For $n\ge D$, the actual sum is $A+F(n-D)$. Keep the same standard Brownian motion $W$ and use $A+F(n-D)-\kappa W(n)=A+[F(n-D)-\kappa W(n-D)]+\kappa[W(n-D)-W(n)]$. The fixed-window Brownian estimates in step 4.1 hold on one event for every positive integer window length. On that event choose an integer at least the finite random $D$; then $\max_{D\le k\le n}|W(k-D)-W(k)|=O(\sqrt{\log n})$, regardless of any dependence of $D$ and $W$. Finitely many earlier indices contribute a finite maximum. Steps 4.3 and 5.1 therefore give the complete-path bound $\max_{k\le n}|\sum_{i=1}^k f(X_i)-\kappa W(k)|=o(n^b)$ in the factor construction. Neither a moment of the initial law nor an assertion that a randomly shifted Brownian path is standard has been used.

Identify $\kappa$ without making an unsupported second-moment inference from the almost-sure approximation. Use the same factor and fixed post-delay tour law under invariant initial law, as supplied in [F1]–[F2]. Steps 1.2–5.2 then give a CLT with variance $\kappa^2=u/\mu$: the approximation error divided by $\sqrt n$ tends to zero almost surely since $b<1/2$, and $\kappa W(n)/\sqrt n$ has exactly the centered normal law of variance $\kappa^2$ for each $n$; apply [F12]'s converging-together result. Independently, [F11] gives exponential stationary strong mixing of the original observations. Their $Q_0$th moment, with $Q_0>2$, satisfies [F12]'s moment regime because every positive power of an exponential rate is summable. Hence [F12] gives the stationary CLT with its absolutely convergent covariance-sum variance $\sigma_g^2$, the asymptotic variance in the Statement's convention. The stationary observation-path equality in [F1] makes these two limits refer to the same law. Uniqueness of centered normal characteristic functions, $e^{-t^2\kappa^2/2}=e^{-t^2\sigma_g^2/2}$, gives $\kappa^2=\sigma_g^2$. The assumed positivity therefore gives $\kappa=\sigma_g>0$. This argument uses no uniform-integrability assumption on the approximation error.

Finally preserve the actual original chain probability space. The factor construction gives a joint law of its real observation sequence and the rational-time coordinates of the final standard Brownian motion $W$. Both are standard-Borel real sequence spaces by [F8]. Use [F1]'s lifting assertion, or disintegrate this joint law and apply its conditional kernel at the actual sequence $(f(X_1),f(X_2),\ldots)$ by [F8]; this preserves the entire original probability space and reproduces that observation/Gaussian-coordinate joint law. The approximation event uses only these observations and integer driver coordinates, so it still has probability one. The rational coordinates extend to a continuous Brownian path on a common measurable full-measure event: for each positive integers $M,k$, some integer $l$ makes all rational pairs in $[0,M]$ at distance below $1/l$ have coordinate difference below $1/k$. This is a Borel condition and has probability one under the original Brownian rational law; completeness of $\mathbb R$ gives a unique consistent continuous extension on compact intervals. Every fixed real-time evaluation is the limit along a deterministic rational sequence, hence measurable; on the null failure event set the path to zero. Its finite-dimensional laws agree with standard Brownian laws by continuity, so [F10] identifies genuine standard Brownian motion on the extension. With $B=W$, steps 5.2–6.1 give error $o(n^{1/p})$, and $p>P_0$ implies $n^{1/p}/(n^{1/P_0}\log n)\to0$. Choosing the finite eventual bound and starting index in this almost-sure comparison gives precisely the $C(\omega),N(\omega)$ in the Statement. AC was used through the stated local Gaussian, factor, tour and extension suppliers; the full moment range, arbitrary initial law, positive-variance convention and original observation indices are retained.

boundaries.evidence: The state space carries an invariant probability and is nonempty. Empty partial sums, zero-count Poisson subintervals and initial finite index ranges are covered; the target is eventual in n.

The Statement retains σ_g>0. Internally, zero residual variance is handled in steps 1.2/3.3, zero length variance in step 5.1, and zero full Gaussian covariance before variance identification in step 6.1. No division by a zero variance is used.

Unit Poisson counts are interpolated with their actual conditional uniform event-time law in step 2.1; their O(log n) maximum and within-unit Brownian oscillations are proved in step 2.2. Tour lengths are positive integers and incomplete endpoint cycles are retained.

The joint Gaussian covariance may be singular. Regression uses full long-run Γ12; covariance-zero clock and reward directions are handled explicitly. Initial prefix dependence on tail seeds and Brownian driver is permitted: step 5.2 uses the same driver with a finite-window path bound.

P0=2+δ<p<q<Q0=2+δ+ε makes b=1/p<1/P0<1/2. The scalar clock exponent r>p is chosen with all required Poisson/exponential moments, rather than claiming a logarithmic KMT rate. Strict inverse endpoint counts use floor(t/γ)+1 and the bounded eighth remainder.

AC is explicit in the Facts and proposed axiom_use. The measurable factor preserves arbitrary initial observation laws, standard-Borel kernels glue the actual Gaussian drivers, and the final lift conditions only on real observations/rational Brownian coordinates; no arbitrary-state RCD is assumed.

boundaries.reason: The theorem is a one-way sufficient-condition assertion, not a biconditional.
No converse geometric-ergodicity, moment or strong-approximation claim is made.

risk_review.notes: Complete local proof replaces the escalation paragraph while preserving the original Statement and frontmatter bytes. Exact inputs include the final same-tour-law clause, joint adjacent-iid Gaussian approximation, high-moment scalar iid clock couplings, locally proved Haar composition, centered one-dependent moving windows, covariance CLT identification and original-space path-law lift. No external SIP, scalar-independent-driver shortcut, iid full-tour assumption, uniform-integrability shortcut or random-shifted-Wiener-law claim is used.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume Choice. For every probability measure $\mu$ and probability kernel $K$
on an arbitrary measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$, the canonical path space
$$ (E^{\mathbb N_0},\mathcal E^{\otimes\mathbb N_0}) $$
carries a unique probability $\mathbb P_\mu$ under which the coordinate maps
form a Markov chain with initial law $\mu$ and transition kernel $K$.

Assume AC ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $K$ be a probability kernel on a
measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$, let $\pi$ be an invariant probability for $K$
([[def-invariant-and-stationary-distribution-for-a-markov-kernel]]), and let
$X$ be a $K$-chain with initial law $\pi$
([[def-initial-distribution-of-a-markov-chain]]). Then every finite-dimensional
law of $X$ is invariant under every nonnegative integer time shift: for every
$r\ge1$, every $0\le n_1<\cdots<n_r$ and every $m\ge0$,

$$\mathcal L(X_{m+n_1},\ldots,X_{m+n_r})=\mathcal L(X_{n_1},\ldots,X_{n_r}).$$

Equivalently, the canonical path law
$\mathbb P_X:=\mathcal L\bigl((X_n)_{n\ge0}\bigr)$ on
$(E^{\mathbb N_0},\mathcal E^{\otimes\mathbb N_0})$ is invariant under the left
shift $\theta(z)_n=z_{n+1}$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $P$ be a probability kernel on a measurable space
$(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ with invariant probability $\pi$. Assume it is
$\phi$-irreducible
([[def-phi-irreducible-chain]]), aperiodic
([[def-general-state-aperiodic-markov-chain]]), and Harris recurrent relative
to its nonzero $\sigma$-finite irreducibility measure $\phi$
([[def-harris-recurrent-markov-chain]]). Suppose $P$ is geometrically
ergodic in the sense of
[[def-geometric-and-uniform-ergodicity-for-mcmc-clt]]. Then there exist a
measurable $M:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ with $\pi(M)<\infty$ and $r\in(0,1)$ such
that
$$\|P^n(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le M(x)r^n\quad(x\in\mathsf X,\ n\ge1).$$

In fact, the same conclusion holds assuming only AC, invariance of $\pi$, and the everywhere finite measurable common geometric-rate bound in [[def-geometric-and-uniform-ergodicity-for-mcmc-clt]], on the original arbitrary measurable space. The construction below derives the needed irreducibility on a restricted sigma-field directly from that bound.

Assume AC. Let $(X_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a stationary time-homogeneous Markov chain
with invariant probability $\pi$. Suppose there are a measurable
$M:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ with $\pi(M)<\infty$ and $r\in(0,1)$ such that
$$\|P^n(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le M(x)r^n\quad\text{for every }x\in\mathsf X,\ n\ge1.$$
Then the strong-mixing coefficient of the stationary process satisfies
$$\alpha_X(n)\le\pi(M)r^n\quad(n\ge1).$$

Let $X=(X_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a strictly stationary process on a measurable state
space and let $h$ be a measurable real-valued function. Put $Y_k=h(X_k)$.
Then $Y$ is strictly stationary and, for every $n\ge1$,
$$\alpha_Y(n)\le\alpha_X(n),\qquad \phi_Y(n)\le\phi_X(n),\qquad \rho_Y(n)\le\rho_X(n),$$
where the coefficients are as in
[[def-mixing-coefficients-for-stationary-markov-chain]].

Assume AC. Let $(Y_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a centered strictly stationary real sequence with $\mathbb E[Y_0^2]<\infty$, and define $S_n=\sum_{k=1}^nY_k$. Each of the following is sufficient:

1. There is $B<\infty$ with $|Y_0|\le B$ almost surely and $\sum_{n\ge1}\alpha_Y(n)<\infty$.
2. For some $\delta>0$, $\mathbb E|Y_0|^{2+\delta}<\infty$ and $\sum_{n\ge1}\alpha_Y(n)^{\delta/(2+\delta)}<\infty$.
3. For some $a\in(0,1)$, $\alpha_Y(n)=O(a^n)$ and $\mathbb E[Y_0^2\log^+|Y_0|]<\infty$, where $\log^+u=\max(0,\log u)$ for $u>0$ and $0\log^+0:=0$.

In each case the covariance series
$$\sigma_Y^2:=\mathbb E[Y_0^2]+2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\operatorname{Cov}(Y_0,Y_k)$$
converges absolutely and is nonnegative, and
$$n^{-1/2}S_n\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma_Y^2).$$
This includes the degenerate law $N(0,0)$ when $\sigma_Y^2=0$, as in [[lem-zero-long-run-variance-gives-degenerate-clt]]. The coefficient $\alpha_Y$ and strict stationarity have the meanings in [[def-mixing-coefficients-for-stationary-markov-chain]].

Let $(X_k)_{k\ge0}$ be a stationary time-homogeneous Markov chain with invariant probability $\pi$, and let $f$ be real Borel with $\pi(f)=0$ and $\pi(f^2)<\infty$. For $k\ge0$, set $\gamma_k:=\operatorname{Cov}_{\pi}(f(X_0),f(X_k))$. When the Markov-chain CLT $n^{-1/2}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}f(X_k)\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma_f^2)$ holds with finite variance parameter and $\sum_{k\ge1}|\gamma_k|<\infty$, the **covariance long-run variance** is
$$\sigma^2_{\mathrm{LR}}(f):=\gamma_0+2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\gamma_k.$$

This definition does not infer a CLT from covariance summability, or infer that a weak-limit variance equals the covariance sum. Whenever $\sigma^2_{\mathrm{LR}}(f)$ is used as the variance parameter in a CLT or MCSE claim, that equality must be established by the theorem being applied. For example, the local Poisson-equation theorem proves the equality under its square-integrable solution hypotheses.

Let $P$ be a geometrically ergodic Markov chain with invariant probability
$\pi$, let $g$ be real Borel, and suppose there are $\delta,\varepsilon>0$
with $\pi(|g|^{2+\delta+\varepsilon})<\infty$. Suppose also that a
state-dependent one-step minorization
[[def-state-dependent-one-step-minorization]] holds. For the Flegal–Jones
strong invariance principle convention, assume its asymptotic standard
deviation satisfies $0<\sigma_g<\infty$. Then on a suitable extension of the
chain's probability space there are a standard Brownian motion $B$, a finite
random constant $C(\omega)$, and a finite random index $N(\omega)$ such that
for all $n\ge N(\omega)$,
$$\left|\sum_{i=1}^n(g(X_i)-\pi(g))-\sigma_g B(n)\right|\le C(\omega)n^{1/(2+\delta)}\log n$$
almost surely.

Assume AC. Let $P$ be a probability kernel on an arbitrary measurable space $(\mathsf X,\mathcal X)$ with invariant probability $\pi$. Suppose its stationary Markov chain has strong-mixing coefficients $\alpha_X(n)\le Cr^n$ for $n\ge1$, with $0\le C<\infty$ and $0<r<1$. Let $f:\mathsf X\to\mathbb R$ be finite measurable with $\pi f=0$, $\pi|f|^q<\infty$ for a finite $q>2$, and suppose the absolutely convergent covariance sum is zero:
$$v:=\pi(f^2)+2\sum_{n\ge1}\operatorname{Cov}_\pi(f(X_0),f(X_n))=0.$$
Then for every $2<p<q$, under the stationary law,
$$\max_{0\le j\le n}\left|\sum_{k=0}^{j-1}f(X_k)\right|=o(n^{1/p})\qquad\text{almost surely}.$$
The empty sum at $j=0$ is zero. No ergodicity assumption is needed beyond the stated stationary mixing bound.

If additionally $\|P^n(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\to0$ for every $x\in\mathsf X$, the same assertion holds under every initial probability law, without a moment assumption on that law. In particular, it holds under every initial law whenever $P$ has an everywhere finite measurable common geometric total-variation envelope in the sense of [[def-geometric-and-uniform-ergodicity-for-mcmc-clt]] and $f$ has the stated moment, centering and zero covariance sum. No positive one-step minorization, irreducibility or Harris hypothesis is added to this last sufficient condition.

Assume AC. Let $Y_1,Y_2,\ldots$ be real random variables and $S_k=\sum_{i=1}^kY_i$, with $S_0=0$. Suppose on a probability-space extension with the original process as marginal there are a standard Brownian motion $B$, constants $\sigma\ge0$ and $0<\alpha<1/2$, and finite random constants $K,N$ such that almost surely
$$|S_k-\sigma B(k)|\le K k^\alpha\log k\qquad(k\ge N).$$
Let $(b_n)$ be deterministic positive integers with $b_n<n$ eventually and
$$\frac{b_n}{n}\to0,\qquad \sum_{n=2}^\infty(b_n/n)^c<\infty\quad\text{for some real }c\ge1,$$
$$\frac{b_n\log n}{n}\to0,\qquad\frac{n^{2\alpha}(\log n)^2}{b_n}\to0.$$
For the exact estimator of [[alg-overlapping-batch-means-mcse]], applied to $Y_1,\ldots,Y_n$,
$$\widehat\sigma_{\mathrm{OBM},n}^2=\frac{nb_n}{(n-b_n)(n-b_n+1)}\sum_{j=0}^{n-b_n}\left(\frac{S_{j+b_n}-S_j}{b_n}-\frac{S_n}{n}\right)^2\longrightarrow\sigma^2\quad\text{almost surely}.$$
No stationarity, independence of $B$ from $(Y_i)$, or monotonicity of $b_n$ or $n/b_n$ is required. The conclusion includes $\sigma=0$.

Let $\delta>0$ and let $(b_n)_{n\ge2}$ be positive integers. Say that the sequence satisfies the **Flegal–Jones OBM batch-size conditions for exponent $\delta$**, with the integer monotonicity correction described below, when $b_n<n$ for all sufficiently large $n$, $b_n\to\infty$, $n/b_n\to\infty$, and there is a constant $c\ge1$ such that
$$\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}(b_n/n)^c<\infty,$$
while
$$\frac{b_n}{n}\log n\to0,\qquad \frac{n^{2/(2+\delta)}(\log n)^3}{b_n}\to0,$$
there are $n_0\ge2$ and $c_1<\infty$ with $\log n/b_n\le c_1$ for all $n\ge n_0$, and
$$b_n^2n^{-2}\log\log n\to0,\qquad b_n^4n^{-3}\log\log n\to0.$$

These are all the numerical rate, summability and endpoint hypotheses of Flegal–Jones Theorem 2. The source additionally asks that both $b_n$ and $n/b_n$ be nondecreasing. Those two requirements are omitted here: for an integer sequence with $b_n<n$ eventually they are incompatible with $b_n\to\infty$. Indeed, ratio monotonicity would imply $n(b_{n+1}-b_n)\le b_n<n$, while integer monotonicity would force the nonnegative integer $b_{n+1}-b_n$ to be zero. Thus the literal source conditions would make $b_n$ eventually constant. The corrected interface preserves the intended floor-power batch sequences, and the Brownian quadratic-form proof of OBM consistency needs neither monotonicity assumption.

This is a sufficient-condition interface; failure of a condition does not imply inconsistency of the estimator.

For the floor-power sequence $b_n=\lfloor n^\nu\rfloor$, the intended source range $\delta>2/3$ and $2/(2+\delta)<\nu<3/4$ satisfies this corrected contract. Indeed, eventually $n^\nu/2\le b_n\le n^\nu$. Choose $c>\max\{1,1/(1-\nu)\}$ to bound the summability series by $\sum_n n^{-c(1-\nu)}<\infty$. The other displayed quantities are bounded respectively by $n^{\nu-1}\log n$, $2n^{2/(2+\delta)-\nu}(\log n)^3$, $2n^{-\nu}\log n$, $n^{2\nu-2}\log\log n$ and $n^{4\nu-3}\log\log n$, all tending to zero. Also $b_n\to\infty$, $n/b_n\to\infty$ and $b_n<n$ eventually. These checks establish the numerical contract without asserting the impossible simultaneous monotonicity.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and let $d\ge1$ be finite.

1. A standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion exists: one may take $d$
   independent copies of the constructed one-dimensional Brownian path and
   assemble them coordinatewise.
2. If $B$ is any standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion and $c>0$, then
   $$Y_t=c^{-1/2}B_{ct},\qquad t\ge0,$$
   is again standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion. Moreover, the random
   elements $B$ and $Y$ have the same law on $(\mathbb R^d)^{[0,\infty)}$
   equipped with its cylinder sigma-algebra.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

derivations.claim: Put $q=2+\delta+\varepsilon$, $\mu=\pi(g)$ and $f=g-\mu$. The moment hypothesis gives $\pi|g|<\infty$, since $|g|\le1+|g|^q$, so $\mu$ is finite. The elementary bound $|g-\mu|^q\le2^q(|g|^q+|\mu|^q)$ gives $\pi|f|^q<\infty$, and $\pi f=0$. For variance identification consider the canonical chain with initial law $\pi$, which is stationary by [F1]. The given geometric bound has an everywhere finite measurable common envelope, so the stronger arbitrary-measurable-space clause of [F2] supplies an integrable such envelope. By [F3], this stationary chain and its observation $f$ have a strong-mixing bound $\alpha_f(n)\le Cr^n$ with $C<\infty$ and $r\in(0,1)$. This construction is only for identifying the stationary covariance parameter; the observed initial law remains arbitrary.

Take $\eta=q-2=\delta+\varepsilon>0$. The geometric bound in step 1.1 makes $\sum_n\alpha_f(n)^{\eta/(2+\eta)}$ finite. Apply [F4] to the stationary observed sequence. Its covariance series is absolutely convergent, its sum $v=\pi(f^2)+2\sum_{k\ge1}\operatorname{Cov}_\pi(f(X_0),f(X_k))$ is finite and nonnegative, and its CLT has precisely variance $v$. Thus [F5] identifies $v=\sigma_g^2$, without using the stationary Harris-only formulation of a separate MCMC regime theorem. Write $\sigma=\sqrt v\ge0$ and $\alpha=1/(2+\delta)\in(0,1/2)$.

If $v>0$, the original $g$, the given $\delta,\varepsilon$, geometric ergodicity and supplied minorization meet [F6] with the finite positive standard deviation from step 1.2. Hence, for the original arbitrary initial law, on an extension there are a standard Brownian motion $B$ and finite random constants for which $|\sum_{i=1}^n f(X_i)-\sigma B(n)|=O(n^\alpha\log n)$ almost surely. The same moment exponents and the same covariance variance are used; no stronger moment assumption is introduced.

If $v=0$, choose a real $p$ with $2+\delta<p<q$, possible because $\varepsilon>0$. Apply the all-start geometric-envelope clause of [F7] to $f$; its moment and zero covariance hypotheses were established in steps 1.1–1.2. Use the chain indexed from $X_1$ as its time-zero chain, whose initial law is still arbitrary. Then $\max_{j\le n}|\sum_{i=1}^j f(X_i)|=o(n^{1/p})$ almost surely. Since $1/p<\alpha$, this implies $|\sum_{i=1}^n f(X_i)|=O(n^\alpha\log n)$. Adjoin a standard Brownian motion on the product extension supplied by [F10] and set $\sigma=0$. The same approximation as in step 2.1 now holds, with zero Brownian coefficient. No division by $\sigma$ or implication from a degenerate CLT to an almost-sure rate is used.

In either variance branch the hypotheses of [F8] hold with this $\sigma,\alpha$. Indeed $n/b_n\to\infty$ gives $b_n/n\to0$, while the summability and $(b_n/n)\log n\to0$ assumptions are displayed in the Statement. Moreover $n^{2\alpha}(\log n)^2/b_n=[n^{2/(2+\delta)}(\log n)^3/b_n]/\log n\to0$. The other stated numerical endpoint and growth conditions are retained and impose no additional requirement in this reduction. Thus [F8] gives convergence to $\sigma^2=v$ for the exact OBM estimator applied to $Y_i=f(X_i)$.

Centering the observations by the constant $\mu$ does not change this finite estimator: $\bar f_n=\bar g_n-\mu$ and $\bar f_{n,j}(b_n)=\bar g_{n,j}(b_n)-\mu$, so their difference equals $\bar g_{n,j}(b_n)-\bar g_n$. The indexing $j=0,\ldots,n-b_n$ in [F8] is exactly $j=1,\ldots,n-b_n+1$ after adding one to the starting index, and its denominator is $(n-b_n)(n-b_n+1)$ as here. Therefore its estimator is the displayed $\widehat\sigma^2_{\mathrm{OBM},n}$, and steps 1.2 and 3.1 prove its almost-sure convergence to $\sigma_g^2$ under the original arbitrary initial law.

Finally, the source-corollary range is $2/(2+\delta)<\nu<3/4$. By [F9], $b_n=\lfloor n^\nu\rfloor$ satisfies every corrected numerical batch hypothesis, so steps 1.1–3.2 apply to it as well. This verifies the intended floor-power conclusion without asserting the incompatible ratio monotonicity. The proof includes $v=0$, finite early inadmissible batch indices, and arbitrary initial laws without additional moment hypotheses, as allowed by [F7]–[F8].

The initial observation X_1 is treated as the time-zero state in step 2.2; the summation and batch-start index shift is checked in step 3.2.
Step 2.2 includes constant observables and zero variance. The proof never divides by sigma or by the estimated variance.

Step 1.2 uses strict delta>0 to put alpha in (0,1/2); epsilon>0 permits the intermediate zero-branch p. Step 3.1 uses eventual 1<=b_n<n and every needed numerical rate; step 4.1 preserves the intended floor range.

manifest_rows.title: Heterogeneous bounded atom vector rows admit a logarithmic cubed Gaussian coupling
manifest_rows.statement:
Assume AC. Fix $K\ge1$ and $A>0$. There is a finite $C_{A,K}$ such that the following holds uniformly over $1\le d\le2$, integers $1\le m\le N$, and $B\ge1$. Let $X_1,\ldots,X_m$ be independent centered vectors with representations
$$X_i=Z_i+\sum_{r=1}^{r_i}Y_{ir},\qquad |Y_{ir}|\le B\ \hbox{almost surely},$$
where every $r_i$ is finite, all displayed atom and Gaussian terms are independent, every $Y_{ir}$ is centered, and every $Z_i$ is a centered Gaussian vector, possibly degenerate. Suppose
$$I_d\le D_i:=\operatorname{cov}(X_i)\le KI_d.$$
There is a coupling with independent $G_i\sim N_d(0,D_i)$ satisfying
$$\Pr\!\left(\max_{1\le k\le m}\left|\sum_{i=1}^k(X_i-G_i)\right|>C_{A,K}B\log^3(eN)\right)\le N^{-A}.$$
The constants do not depend on the atom counts or individual laws. Empty atom sums and zero Gaussian terms are allowed.

The coupling laws can be chosen as a measurable probability kernel in a supplied standard Borel parameter $\theta$: if the atom laws and Gaussian covariance matrices are measurable kernels and functions of $\theta$, with the hypotheses holding for each $\theta$, there is a coupling kernel $Q_\theta(dx,dg)$ with the stated product marginals and the displayed bound for each $\theta$. Thus a random environment with these conditional independent atom laws can first be sampled, and this coupling kernel then applied conditionally. This assertion concerns the conditional laws supplied in the hypotheses and does not assume a selection of regular conditional laws separately at each parameter.

references.title: A. Yu. Zaitsev, Multidimensional version of the results of Komlos, Major and Tusnady for vectors with finite exponential moments (1998), Section 5; heterogeneous covariance interpolation and Gaussian anchor specialization proved here

manifest_rows.title: Adjacent iid vector functionals admit a finite-moment strong approximation
manifest_rows.statement:
Assume AC. Let $1\le d\le2$, let $(E,\mathcal E)$ be standard Borel, and let $(U_i)_{i\ge0}$ be iid $E$-valued random elements with law $\nu$. Let $h:E^2\to\mathbb R^d$ be measurable with
$$\mathbb E h(U_0,U_1)=0,\qquad \mathbb E|h(U_0,U_1)|^q<\infty$$
for some finite $q>2$. Put $X_i=h(U_i,U_{i+1})$, and define
$$\Gamma=\mathbb E[X_0X_0^T]+\mathbb E[X_0X_1^T]+\mathbb E[X_1X_0^T].$$
Then $\Gamma$ is positive semidefinite. For every fixed $2<p<q$, on an extension preserving the entire original process there are independent centered Gaussian vectors $G_i$ with covariance $\Gamma$ such that
$$\max_{1\le k\le n}\left|\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}(X_i-G_i)\right|=o(n^{1/p})\qquad\hbox{almost surely}.$$
The extension can also carry a standard $d$-dimensional Brownian motion $B$ with $\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}G_i=\Gamma^{1/2}B(k)$ for every integer $k\ge0$. Singular $\Gamma$, including $\Gamma=0$, is allowed. Neither the Gaussian row nor $B$ is required to be independent of the original process.

references.title: Istvan Berkes, Weidong Liu and Wei Biao Wu, Komlos-Major-Tusnady approximation under dependence, Annals of Probability 42 (2014), 794–817, Sections 3.2–3.4; adjacent iid specialization and matrix Gaussian redistribution proved locally

A. Yu. Zaitsev, Multidimensional version of the results of Komlos, Major and Tusnady for vectors with finite exponential moments, Sections 5–8; finite-horizon truncation from the locally proved bounded coupling

manifest_rows.title: Strong invariance principle for geometrically ergodic chains
manifest_rows.statement:
Let $P$ be a geometrically ergodic Markov chain with invariant probability
$\pi$, let $g$ be real Borel, and suppose there are $\delta,\varepsilon>0$
with $\pi(|g|^{2+\delta+\varepsilon})<\infty$. Suppose also that a
state-dependent one-step minorization
[[def-state-dependent-one-step-minorization]] holds. For the Flegal–Jones
strong invariance principle convention, assume its asymptotic standard
deviation satisfies $0<\sigma_g<\infty$. Then on a suitable extension of the
chain's probability space there are a standard Brownian motion $B$, a finite
random constant $C(\omega)$, and a finite random index $N(\omega)$ such that
for all $n\ge N(\omega)$,
$$\left|\sum_{i=1}^n(g(X_i)-\pi(g))-\sigma_g B(n)\right|\le C(\omega)n^{1/(2+\delta)}\log n$$
almost surely.

references.title: James M. Flegal and Galin L. Jones, Batch means and spectral variance estimators in Markov chain Monte Carlo, Lemma 3
Florence Merlevède and Emmanuel Rio, Strong approximation for additive functionals of geometrically ergodic Markov chains, Lemma 2.4 and proof roadmap
Elena Bashtova and Alexey Shashkin, Strong Gaussian approximation for cumulative processes with heavy tails, Theorem 1 and calendar-time decomposition

manifest_rows.title: Strong consistency of overlapping batch means
manifest_rows.statement:
Let $P$ be a geometrically ergodic Markov chain with invariant probability $\pi$, and let the initial distribution be arbitrary. Let $g$ be real Borel and suppose $\pi(|g|^{2+\delta+\varepsilon})<\infty$ for some $\delta,\varepsilon>0$. Assume the state-dependent one-step minorization [[def-state-dependent-one-step-minorization]]: there are measurable $s:\mathsf X\to[0,1]$ and a probability measure $Q$ such that $P(x,A)\ge s(x)Q(A)$ for all $x,A$.

Let $(b_n)$ be positive integer batch sizes with $1\le b_n<n$ for all sufficiently large $n$, $b_n\to\infty$, and $n/b_n\to\infty$. Suppose there is $c\ge1$ such that
$$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(b_n/n)^c<\infty,$$
and suppose
$$\frac{b_n}{n}\log n\to0,\qquad \frac{n^{2/(2+\delta)}(\log n)^3}{b_n}\to0,$$
there are $n_0$ and $c_1<\infty$ with $\log n/b_n\le c_1$ for every $n\ge n_0$, and
$$b_n^2n^{-2}\log\log n\to0,\qquad b_n^4n^{-3}\log\log n\to0.$$

For $\bar g_n=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^ng(X_i)$ and $\bar g_{n,j}(b_n)=b_n^{-1}\sum_{i=j}^{j+b_n-1}g(X_i)$, define
$$\widehat\sigma^2_{\mathrm{OBM},n}=\frac{nb_n}{(n-b_n)(n-b_n+1)}\sum_{j=1}^{n-b_n+1}\bigl(\bar g_{n,j}(b_n)-\bar g_n\bigr)^2.$$
The strong-consistency conclusion is
$$\widehat\sigma^2_{\mathrm{OBM},n}\longrightarrow\sigma_g^2\quad\text{almost surely},$$
where $\sigma_g^2$ is the covariance long-run variance defined by [[def-long-run-variance-for-stationary-markov-chain]]. The batch sequence satisfies [[def-flegal-jones-obm-batch-size-conditions]] for the displayed exponent $\delta$; these conditions are written out above. This corrects the source's incompatible requirement that both integer $b_n$ and $n/b_n$ be nondecreasing, retaining every numerical batch-size hypothesis.

As in the intended source corollary, if $\delta>2/3$ and $(1+\delta/2)^{-1}<\nu<3/4$, then $b_n=\lfloor n^\nu\rfloor$ satisfies these corrected batch-size hypotheses and has the same strong-consistency conclusion. No monotonicity of $n/\lfloor n^\nu\rfloor$ is asserted.

references.title: James M. Flegal and Galin L. Jones, Batch means and spectral variance estimators in Markov chain Monte Carlo, Theorem 2 and Appendix B.3
James M. Flegal and Galin L. Jones, Batch means and spectral variance estimators in Markov chain Monte Carlo, Corollary 1

Assume AC. Let $P$ be a probability kernel on an arbitrary measurable space $(X,\mathcal F)$, with invariant probability $\pi$, finite measurable $M:X\to[0,\infty)$ and $0<r<1$ satisfying
$$\|P^n(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le M(x)r^n\quad(x\in X,\ n\ge1).$$
Let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be finite measurable. For each specified initial law $\mu$, there are a nonempty standard-Borel space $S$, a probability kernel $T$ on $S$, an invariant probability $\widehat\pi$, an initial probability $\widehat\mu$, and finite measurable functions $\varphi:S\to\mathbb R$ and $\widehat M:S\to[0,\infty)$ such that
$$\|T^n(z,\cdot)-\widehat\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le\widehat M(z)r^n\quad(z\in S,\ n\ge1).$$
The complete observation path $(f(X_n))_{n\ge0}$ of a $\mu$-started $P$-chain has the same law as $(\varphi(Y_n))_{n\ge0}$ of a $\widehat\mu$-started $T$-chain. The corresponding stationary observation paths also have the same law, and $\widehat\pi(|\varphi|^a)=\pi(|f|^a)$ for every $a>0$, with infinity allowed. The factor may depend on $\mu$.

Moreover, any joint law of that observation path with a random element of a standard-Borel space can be lifted to an extension preserving the entire original chain probability space and process.

already_integrated_supplier_context.current_statement_exact:
Assume AC. Let $P$ be a probability kernel on a nonempty standard-Borel space $(S,\mathcal S)$, with invariant probability $\pi$, finite measurable $M:S\to[0,\infty)$ and $0<r<1$ such that
$$\|P^n(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le M(x)r^n\quad(x\in S,\ n\ge1).$$
Let $f:S\to\mathbb R$ be finite measurable, with $\pi(f)=0$ and $\pi(|f|^v)<\infty$ for some $v>1$. For every initial law, on an extension preserving the given chain there are an integer $m\ge1$, an almost surely finite delay $D\in m\mathbb N$, a standard-Borel seed space $E$, iid seeds $(U_j)_{j\ge0}$, and measurable finite-word and length functions $W:E^2\to\bigsqcup_{k\ge1}S^k$ and $L:E\to m\mathbb N$ with the following properties.

Put $T_0=D$ and $T_{j+1}=T_j+L(U_j)$. Almost surely, simultaneously for all $j\ge0$,
$$\bigl(X_{T_j},\ldots,X_{T_{j+1}-1}\bigr)=W(U_j,U_{j+1}).$$
Write $L_j=L(U_j)$, $Z_j=\sum_{t=T_j}^{T_{j+1}-1}f(X_t)$, and $H_j=\sum_{t=T_j}^{T_{j+1}-1}|f(X_t)|$. Then $Z_j=z(U_j,U_{j+1})$ and $H_j=h(U_j,U_{j+1})$ for measurable functions $z,h$, and
$$\mathbb E e^{aL_0}<\infty\text{ for some }a>0,\qquad 0<\mu_L:=\mathbb EL_0<\infty,$$
$$\mathbb EZ_0=0,\qquad \mathbb EH_0^q<\infty\quad(1\le q<v).$$
For every nonnegative measurable $b:S\to[0,\infty]$ the full-tour occupation identity is
$$\mathbb E\sum_{t=T_0}^{T_1-1}b(X_t)=\mu_L\pi(b).$$
For each specified initial law, the same $m$, iid seed law, $W,L$ and post-delay tour law can be used also for the invariant initial law $\pi$; only the finite initial segment and coupling change.

In particular $(L_j-\mu_L,Z_j)$ is an adjacent-iid centered vector sequence, while the lengths themselves are iid. Full tour words or rewards are not asserted to be iid. No moment of $D$ or of the initial finite prefix is required, and the construction uses a useful multistep split chosen from $P$ rather than requiring any supplied one-step minorization to have positive stationary mass.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $Q$ be a probability kernel on any measurable space $(X,\mathcal G)$, with invariant probability $\pi$. Let $C\in\mathcal G$ satisfy $\pi(C)>0$, and suppose
$$Q(x,\cdot)\ge\epsilon\nu(\cdot)\quad(x\in C),\qquad 0<\epsilon<1,$$
where $\nu$ is a probability measure. Suppose some $A<\infty$ and $0<\theta<1$ satisfy
$$|\nu Q^n(C)-\pi(C)|\le A\theta^n\quad(n\ge0).$$
For a $Q$-chain started at $x$, put $\sigma_C=\inf\{n\ge0:X_n\in C\}$. Then some $s>1$ makes
$$H(x)=\mathbb E_x[s^{\sigma_C}]\quad\text{measurable},\qquad \pi(H)<\infty,$$
where $s^\infty=\infty$. In particular $H$ is finite $\pi$-almost everywhere; finiteness at every state is not asserted.

For the same hypotheses, the split construction also has the following return and occupation properties. Put $w_1(x)=\epsilon1_C(x)$ and $w_0(x)=1-w_1(x)$. Define $K_{x,1}=\nu$, $K_{x,0}=(Q(x,\cdot)-\epsilon\nu)/(1-\epsilon)$ on $C$, and $K_{x,0}=Q(x,\cdot)$ off $C$. On $X\times\{0,1\}$ use the kernel
$$\widetilde Q((x,i),dy\times\{j\})=K_{x,i}(dy)w_j(y)$$
and invariant law $\widetilde\pi(dx,i)=w_i(x)\pi(dx)$. Its atom $\alpha=C\times\{1\}$ has mass $p=\epsilon\pi(C)>0$. If $Z_0$ has law $\kappa=\widetilde\pi(\cdot\mid\alpha)$ and $\tau=\inf\{n\ge1:Z_n\in\alpha\}$, then some $b>1$ satisfies
$$\mathbb E_\kappa b^\tau<\infty,$$
and for every nonnegative measurable $g$ on the split space,
$$\widetilde\pi(g)=p\,\mathbb E_\kappa\sum_{k=0}^{\tau-1}g(Z_k).$$
In particular $\tau<\infty$ almost surely and $\mathbb E_\kappa\tau=1/p$. These additional assertions use exactly the construction and hypotheses above; they do not assert an exponential entrance-time moment from every state.

page.current_body_exact:
## Summary

This page defines covariance long-run variance, three stationary mixing coefficients, geometric and polynomial total-variation rates, one-step minorization, and the overlapping-batch-means estimator. It proves the kernel conditional-moment lemma, rate-to-mixing bounds, measurable-factor bounds, the degenerate zero-variance reduction, and the Poisson-equation martingale CLT with its covariance identity.

The six MCMC CLT regimes from Jones (2004) are proved locally with their moment, reversibility and rate-envelope hypotheses. Their suppliers prove the bounded and unbounded strong-mixing limits, the rho and uniform-mixing limits, the reversible geometric correlation bound and the integrable geometric envelope. The Flegal–Jones OBM contract retains every numerical batch-size condition and corrects the source's incompatible simultaneous monotonicity requirements for integer batches. Local Gaussian quadratic-form bounds and a pathwise Brownian-approximation comparison prove the OBM reduction, including zero approximation variance and the exact floor-power batch calculation. The full Markov-chain OBM theorem combines the positive-variance strong approximation with the separate zero-variance strong rate, applies under arbitrary initial laws, and identifies its covariance long-run variance through the stationary mixing CLT. A finite second moment alone is not presented as a CLT criterion, and covariance summability is not used to identify a CLT variance without a theorem.
